## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  ----------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module                  Analysis and Deep Learning on Geometric Data
  Code                    CSC_53431_EP
  Team and workload       Instructor: Maks Ovsjanikov (École Polytechnique, LIX — Geometric Data Analysis group) · 24 h · 2 ECTS · discrete differential geometry, shape operators, functional maps, then deep learning on surfaces: classification, correspondence, parameterization.
  Period                  M2 · period 1 (master's wiki)
  Status in the program   [M2]{.badge .m2} M2 program being finalized by the course instructors (the wiki indicates that the detailed M2 curriculum is still under development); course unit description confirmed by the wiki, SynapseS 2026-2027 sheet not yet published (the S3/S4 tracks of the catalog are currently empty).
  ----------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: an engineer comfortable with GNNs and meshes who wants the geometric operators behind shape analysis (the Laplacian, functional maps).

**Empirical first**: we start from what fails in practice — a shape-matching accuracy that collapses (from about 82% to 51% in a typical lab run) as soon as the mesh is remeshed, a 3D network that ignores curvature — and only then name the tools that fix it: the spectrum, functional maps, networks on surfaces.

The module goes from discrete differential geometry to deep learning on surfaces, following the work of Maks Ovsjanikov's Geometric Data Analysis (GDA) group.

### What you will be able to do

-   Discretize the notions of differential geometry on meshes.
-   Compute and interpret the Laplace-Beltrami operator and the spectrum of a shape.
-   Build shape descriptors and distances that are comparable across surfaces.
-   Put shapes in correspondence through functional maps.
-   Parameterize and process surfaces to make them usable.
-   Train networks that operate directly on surfaces.
-   Understand Euclidean equivariance and its role in geometric learning.

### Official objectives and syllabus

**Official description** (master's wiki): the SynapseS 2026-2027 sheet of this course unit is not yet published (the S3/S4 tracks of the catalog are currently empty); the description confirmed below is that of the wiki, which specifies the volume (24 h), credits (2 ECTS) and instructor.

An introduction to advanced topics in the modern analysis of geometric data, centered on a) the mathematical foundations — discrete differential geometry, mapping, optimization — and b) deep learning for the state-of-the-art methods: a panorama of the foundations of shape analysis and processing, then a move to modern deep-learning-based techniques to solve problems such as shape classification, correspondence and parameterization.

### Where this course fits in the program

M2 module (period 1), 24 h for 2 ECTS, mandatory for every LLGA student.

**Prerequisites**: [Graph Machine and Deep Learning for Generative AI](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html) (mandatory; its spectral graph Laplacian foreshadows the Laplace-Beltrami operator) and a Deep Learning course. [Digital Representation and Analysis of Shapes](../m1p1-shapes/index.html) and [Signal Processing](../m1p1-signal-processing/index.html) help if you took them, but they are not required: the boxes of chapter 0 (meshes, Fourier and heat, optimal transport) give what this page uses from them.

**If you took Shapes** (AI-systems route): you have already seen most of sessions 2–4 (Shapes ch. 5, 7 and 8). Skim ch. 1–3 for the proofs and the notation, then spend the time on functional maps and learning (ch. 4–7).

**Canonical statements.** Other LLGA pages link here instead of re-deriving: [discrete Gauss–Bonnet](#gdl-gauss-bonnet), [the mean-curvature normal](#gdl-mean-curvature), [the cotangent Laplacian from the Dirichlet energy](#gdl-cotangent) and [the HKS with its stability bound](#gdl-hks).

Downstream, it prepares [Graph Generative Models and Applications](../m2-graph-generative-models/index.html) — where 3D molecules become graphs to be generated — and is one of the entry routes toward the research track of the master.

### Course outline

-   **Reminders: spectrum, surfaces, vector calculus** — the mathematics of the module, put back in hand on surface examples.
-   **Discrete differential geometry** — transposing curvatures and derivatives to the discrete world of meshes.
-   **The Laplace-Beltrami operator** — the central spectral operator of shape analysis.
-   **Shape descriptors and distances** — comparing surfaces through computable signatures.
-   **Functional maps** — putting shapes in correspondence by transporting functions.
-   **Parameterization and processing** — flattening and parameterizing surfaces to process them.
-   **Deep learning on surfaces** — defining and training networks directly on geometry.
-   **Euclidean equivariance** — building models that respect the symmetries of space.
-   **Applications and LLGA connections** — where geometry meets the other tracks of the master, with three worked bridges to graphs and language (self-study).
-   **Course research notes — Geometric Data Analysis (Ovsjanikov)** — the papers of the Geometric Data Analysis group, read with the tools of the module (self-study).
-   **Exercises** — spectral computations and correspondences to carry out on real meshes.
-   **Projects and assessment** — solo and group project subjects, a written-exam proposal and a grading rubric.
-   **References** — the foundational papers of geometric analysis and learning on shapes.

### How to study this module

-   Connect each new operator to its graph cousin: the Graph ML Laplacian is the best anchor point of the module.
-   Visualize: eigenfunctions of the Laplace-Beltrami operator, heat kernels, and descriptors are understood as colors on a mesh.
-   Implement the descriptors on small meshes before moving on to full datasets.
-   Redo chapter 0 without hesitation: vector calculus and spectra are used in every chapter.
-   Read the foundational papers on functional maps after the corresponding chapter — the course provides a guided reading of them.
-   Look early at the applications of chapter 8 and the research notes of chapter 9: that is where internship and research topics take shape.

## 0. Reminders: spectrum, surfaces, vector calculus {#ch0}

Every later chapter rests on three pieces of mathematics: the spectral theorem for symmetric matrices, the notion of a surface, and integration by parts on it. This chapter recalls them, with proofs, and sets up the Fourier analogy that the module follows.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
L3/M1 prerequisites mobilized
:::

-   **Differential calculus**: gradient, divergence, Laplacian in $\mathbb{R}^2$ ($\Delta f = \partial_{xx} f + \partial_{yy} f$); Green's formula;
-   **Symmetric diagonalization**: $L = U\Lambda U^\top$, orthonormal basis of eigenfunctions — already seen for the *graph* Laplacian (Graph ML module, ch. 0);
-   **Convolution & Fourier** (Signal Processing, if you took it — the essentials are recalled at the end of this chapter): the Laplacian is the frequency operator; heat diffusion $\partial_t u = \Delta u$;
-   **GNN** (Graph ML module): a mesh *is* a graph — but a geometric one (3D positions, metric).
::::

::: thm
[Theorem 0.1 — Spectral (reminder with proof)]{.tag} If $A \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ is symmetric, its eigenvalues are real and there exists an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors:
$$A = U \Lambda U^\top .$$
Moreover the Rayleigh quotient satisfies
$$R(x) = \frac{x^\top A\, x}{x^\top x}, \qquad \lambda_{\min} = \min_{x \ne 0} R(x), \quad \lambda_{\max} = \max_{x \ne 0} R(x).$$
:::

::: proof
Standard sketch. $R$ is continuous on the (compact) unit sphere, so it attains its maximum at some $u_1$, $\|u_1\| = 1$.

On the sphere, the critical points of $R$ satisfy $Au = R(u)\,u$ (set the gradient of $x^\top A x$ to zero under the constraint $x^\top x = 1$, Lagrange multipliers): $u_1$ is an eigenvector.

Iterate on the orthogonal complement of $u_1$, which is stable under $A$ by symmetry:
$$\langle Au_1, v\rangle = \lambda_1\langle u_1, v\rangle = 0 .$$
This yields the basis by recursion.

The characterization of $\lambda_{\min}$/$\lambda_{\max}$ follows from $R(x) = \sum_k \lambda_k c_k^2$ with $\sum_k c_k^2 = 1$ (barycenter of the $\lambda_k$). [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: prop
[Generalized problem — the one Laplacian object of the page]{.tag} Geometric operators give a pair $(L_c, M)$: a symmetric positive semi-definite *stiffness* matrix $L_c$ (the cotangent matrix of ch. 1–2) and a positive definite diagonal *mass* matrix $M$ (vertex areas). One solves
$$L_c\,\phi = \lambda M\phi, \qquad 0 = \lambda_1 < \lambda_2 \le \dots \quad (\text{1-based, as for graphs; connected mesh}).$$
Setting $\tilde L = M^{-1/2}L_cM^{-1/2}$ (symmetric!), thm. 0.1 applies and $\phi = M^{-1/2}\tilde\phi$; the $\phi_k$ are $M$-orthonormal.

The smooth Laplacian $\Delta_{\mathcal M} = \mathrm{div}\,\nabla$ is negative semi-definite, and its discrete version is $-M^{-1}L_c$.

In the labs, libigl returns the *negative* semi-definite matrix, so negate it once and pass $L_c$ to scipy: `L_c = -igl.cotmatrix(v, f)`, then `eigsh(L_c, k, M=M, sigma=-1e-8)`.
:::

::: def
[Definition 0.2 — Surface, charts, atlas]{.tag} A *surface* (2-dimensional manifold) is a set covered by **charts**: bijections $x : U \subset \mathbb{R}^2 \to V \subset \mathcal M$ whose chart transitions $x_2^{-1} \circ x_1$ are smooth. The collection of charts is an **atlas**.

*Example: the sphere.* Two stereographic charts (from the North pole and the South pole) suffice; on their intersection, the chart transition is the inversion $u \mapsto u/\|u\|^2$ — smooth.

A function $f : \mathcal M \to \mathbb{R}$ is smooth if $f \circ x$ is in every chart; intrinsic quantities (lengths, areas, Laplacian) do not depend on the chosen chart.
:::

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Triangle meshes in one box (for students who did not take Shapes)
:::

-   **Arrays**: a mesh is stored as `V`, an $n \times 3$ float array of vertex positions, and `F`, an $m \times 3$ integer array of vertex indices, one row per triangle. A consistent order of the three indices orients each face, and the normal follows the right-hand rule.
-   **Half-edge structure**: each edge is split into two oriented half-edges. Each half-edge stores its twin, the next half-edge of its face, its origin vertex and its face, so walking around a vertex or a face costs $O(1)$ per step. This is how Shapes ch. 1 and libraries such as OpenMesh or CGAL traverse one-rings; libigl keeps only `V` and `F` and builds adjacency arrays on demand.
-   **Manifold mesh**: every edge belongs to one face (boundary) or two faces (interior), and the faces around each vertex form one fan, a disk or a half-disk. The cotangent Laplacian of ch. 2 assumes this; a non-manifold edge shared by three faces breaks it.
-   **Euler characteristic**: $\chi = |V| - |E| + |F|$. For a closed orientable surface of genus $g$, $\chi = 2 - 2g$ (sphere 2, torus 0), and a closed triangle mesh has $3|F| = 2|E|$. Ch. 1 shows that $\chi$ fixes the total curvature.
::::

::: prop
[Proposition 0.3 — Vector calculus: Green's formula and self-adjointness]{.tag} Gradient (direction of steepest slope), divergence (outgoing flux per unit area), $\Delta f = \mathrm{div}\,\nabla f$.

Green's formula (geometric integration by parts),
$$\int_{\Omega} \langle \nabla f, \nabla g\rangle\, dA = -\int_\Omega f\,\Delta g\, dA + \oint_{\partial\Omega} f\,\partial_n g\, ds,$$
is *the* reason why the Laplacian is symmetric. On a *closed* surface (without boundary),
$$\int f \Delta g = \int g \Delta f$$
— and this symmetry carries over to the discrete setting (ch. 2).
:::

| Euclidean $\mathbb{R}^n$ | Surface $\mathcal M$ |
|---|---|
| translations/rotations | isometries of $\mathcal M$ |
| exponentials $e^{i\langle \omega, x\rangle}$ | eigenfunctions $\phi_k$ of $\Delta_{\mathcal M}$ |
| frequencies $\|\omega\|^2$ | eigenvalues $\lambda_k$ |
| convolution (translation invariant) | operators that are functions of $\Delta_{\mathcal M}$ |
| low-pass filter | attenuating the high $\lambda_k$ |

**Convolution and Fourier (reminder).** Convolution $(f * g)(x) = \int f(x-y)g(y)dy$ is the unique commutative, bilinear, continuous, translation-invariant product. The Fourier transform diagonalizes it:
$$\widehat{f*g} = \hat f \cdot \hat g, \qquad \widehat{\Delta f} = -\|\omega\|^2\hat f .$$
This whole machinery *disappears* on a surface (no translation group); the Laplacian — and it alone — plays its role: this is the program of chapters 2–4.

**Heat is a low-pass filter (reminder).** On $\mathbb{R}^n$, the heat equation $\partial_t u = \Delta u$ is solved by convolution with a Gaussian, and in Fourier each frequency is damped:
$$u(t) = G_t * u_0, \qquad G_t(x) = (4\pi t)^{-n/2}e^{-\|x\|^2/4t}, \qquad \hat u(t,\omega) = e^{-t\|\omega\|^2}\,\hat u_0(\omega).$$
High frequencies die first, so diffusing for a time $t$ keeps the details larger than about $\sqrt t$. On a surface, $\|\omega\|^2$ becomes $\lambda_k$ and the damping becomes $e^{-t\lambda_k}$ (Theorem 2.3): the HKS of ch. 3 and DiffusionNet of ch. 6 are built on this filter.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
OT in one page (self-study, read before session 5)
:::

Optimal transport (OT) compares two distributions by the cheapest way of moving one onto the other. It appears in ch. 4 (functional maps as transport), Ex. 12 and the first group project; the full treatment is [Optimal Transport, ch. 1–5](../m1p2-optimal-transport/index.html#ch5).

-   **Kantorovich problem**: for discrete measures with weights $a \in \mathbb{R}^n$, $b \in \mathbb{R}^m$ (each summing to 1) and a cost matrix $c_{ij}$,
    $$\mathrm{OT}(a, b) = \min_{P \in U(a,b)} \sum_{i,j} P_{ij}\,c_{ij}, \qquad U(a,b) = \{P \ge 0 : P\mathbf{1} = a,\ P^\top\mathbf{1} = b\}.$$
    The coupling $P$ is a soft correspondence; it is a linear program.
-   **Wasserstein distance**: with $c_{ij} = d(x_i, y_j)$ the optimum is $W_1(a, b)$, a true distance between distributions of points (for example, distributions of HKS descriptors on two shapes). Adding an entropy term $-\varepsilon H(P)$ gives the Sinkhorn algorithm, a few matrix–vector products per iteration.
-   **Gromov–Wasserstein**: when the two shapes live in different spaces (two poses, no common coordinates), compare their *internal* distance matrices $D^X$, $D^Y$ (geodesic or diffusion):
    $$\mathrm{GW}(a, b) = \min_{P \in U(a,b)} \sum_{i,j,k,l} \big(D^X_{ik} - D^Y_{jl}\big)^2 P_{ij}P_{kl}.$$
    It is a non-convex quadratic problem, solved by iterated linearisation.
-   **In code** (POT library): `ot.emd2(a, b, cost)`, `ot.sinkhorn2(a, b, cost, reg)` and `ot.gromov.gromov_wasserstein2(DX, DY, a, b)`.
::::

## 1. Discrete differential geometry {#ch1}

A computer stores a surface as a mesh of triangles, while curvature, gradients and the Laplacian are defined on smooth surfaces. This chapter transposes these notions to meshes. A concrete scene shows why they matter: to align two scans of the same object, raw XYZ coordinates work when the pose is fixed but break as soon as the object bends; we need *intrinsic* quantities, which do not change under such deformations.

::: note
[What breaks]{.tag} Three classic failures: extrinsic features (coordinates, normals) that change when the shape bends without stretching; a badly discretized Laplacian on a non-manifold mesh; and too few eigenmodes to resolve the details one needs.
:::

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Triangulated surface]{.tag} A mesh $\mathcal M = (V, E, F)$: vertices $v_i \in \mathbb{R}^3$, edges, triangular faces. It is both a *graph* and an approximation of a smooth *surface*; the mixed Voronoi area $A_i$ associates a "zone" with each vertex.
:::

::: prop
[Construction 1.2 — Barycentric Voronoi areas (computation)]{.tag} Each vertex $i$ receives, within each incident triangle, the portion of the Voronoi cell contained in that triangle. Summed up, the dual area is written *per edge*:
$$A_i = \frac{1}{8}\sum_{j \sim i}\big(\cot\alpha_{ij} + \cot\beta_{ij}\big)\,\|v_i - v_j\|^2,$$
where $\alpha_{ij}, \beta_{ij}$ are the angles opposite to edge $(i,j)$.

*Check on a regular triangular lattice of side $a$*: each vertex has 6 neighbors, each edge has two opposite angles of $60°$, hence $\cot\alpha + \cot\beta = 2/\sqrt3$ per edge and
$$A_i = \frac{1}{8}\cdot 6\cdot\frac{2}{\sqrt3}\,a^2 = \frac{\sqrt3\,a^2}{2} = 6 \times \frac{A_T}{3}, \qquad A_T = \frac{\sqrt3\,a^2}{4},$$
that is, exactly one third of the area of each of the six incident triangles.

For *obtuse* triangles, the per-edge formula can become negative: one switches locally to the barycenter ("mixed", Meyer et al. 2003).
:::

::: thm
[Discrete curvature: the Gauss angle deficit]{.tag}
$$K_i = \frac{2\pi - \sum_{f \ni i}\theta_{i,f}}{A_i}$$
(flat ⇒ $K = 0$; cone ⇒ positive; saddle ⇒ negative). This is a *total measure* of Gaussian curvature over the zone $A_i$.
:::

::: proof
Why $2\pi$ minus the sum of the angles? Transport a tangent vector *parallel to itself* around vertex $i$, staying on the faces. Unfold the incident faces one after the other into the plane, so that inside each face and across each edge the vector does not rotate (the faces are flat).

The unfolded faces cover a total angle $\sum_f \theta_{i,f}$ instead of $2\pi$. So when the loop closes, the final vector makes with the initial one an angle equal to the *deficit*:
$$2\pi - \sum_f \theta_{i,f} .$$

Now on a smooth surface, parallel transport around a loop encircling a total Gaussian curvature $\int K\,dA$ rotates by exactly this angle (local Gauss–Bonnet theorem, "transport" equivalent of the *theorema egregium*: curvature is intrinsic). The deficit is therefore the discrete analogue of $\int_{A_i} K\,dA$, hence the density $K_i$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: {#gdl-gauss-bonnet .thm}
[Theorem 1.3 — Discrete Gauss–Bonnet (statement + numerical example)]{.tag}
$$\sum_{i \in V} K_i\, A_i \;=\; \sum_i \Big(2\pi - \sum_{f\ni i}\theta_{i,f}\Big) \;=\; 2\pi\,\chi(\mathcal M), \qquad \chi = |V| - |E| + |F|.$$
The total curvature depends only on the *topology*.

*Example: the cube.* Eight vertices, three squares (faces split into triangles: angles of $\pi/2$) meet at each vertex. The deficit per vertex and the total are
$$2\pi - 3\times\frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{\pi}{2}, \qquad 8 \times \frac{\pi}{2} = 4\pi = 2\pi \times 2$$
— the characteristic of the sphere.

*A useful counterexample*: the torus (donut) has $\chi = 0$: however it is meshed, the positive and negative deficits cancel out exactly.
:::

::: {#gdl-mean-curvature .prop}
[Principal curvatures, mean curvature: via the Laplacian of positions]{.tag} At each point, the normal sections of the surface have extreme curvatures $k_1 \le k_2$ (*principal*); Gaussian curvature $K = k_1k_2$ (the deficit approximates it); mean curvature $H = \frac{k_1+k_2}{2}$.

*Vector* version, computable directly on the mesh, with $\mathbf{n}$ the **outward** unit normal (so that $H = 1/r > 0$ on a sphere of radius $r$):
$$\Delta_{\mathcal M}\, \mathbf{x} = -2H\,\mathbf{n} \qquad\text{(positions }\mathbf{x}(p) \text{ viewed as 3 functions on } \mathcal{M}\text{)}.$$
Check on the unit sphere: the coordinate functions are eigenfunctions, $\Delta x = -2x$, and $\mathbf{n} = \mathbf{x}$, so $H = 1$.

*Justification (sketch).* The vector $-\Delta\mathbf{x}$ is the gradient of area: varying the surface by $\varepsilon\,f\,\mathbf{n}$ changes the area by $\varepsilon \int 2Hf\,dA$ (first variation; minimal surfaces — soap films — are those with $H = 0$). Computing the same derivative by integration by parts (prop. 0.3) brings out $-\Delta\mathbf{x}$; comparing the two yields the formula.

In the discrete setting, with the stiffness $L_c$ and the mass $M$ of ch. 0 (so that $\Delta \approx -M^{-1}L_c$):
$$H_i\,\mathbf{n}_i = \tfrac12\big(M^{-1}L_c\,\mathbf{x}\big)_i .$$
One line of libigl. On a 642-vertex icosphere of radius 1, with the Voronoi mass of the code in ch. 2, it gives $H_i = 1$ at every vertex, pointing outward to within half a degree; with the barycentric mass, $H_i = 1.00 \pm 0.02$.
:::

-   **Normal of a face**: $n_f \propto (v_j - v_i) \times (v_k - v_i)$; vertex normal: area-weighted (or angle-weighted) average;
-   **Barycentric coordinates**: in a triangle $(i,j,k)$, every point can be written $\alpha v_i + \beta v_j + \gamma v_k$, $\alpha + \beta + \gamma = 1$, with $\alpha$ = normalized area of the opposite sub-triangle; they serve to *interpolate* any function from the vertices to the interior of the faces (a mesh carries values only at vertices);
-   **Finite differences vs finite elements**: the "FD" route approximates $\Delta f$ by combinations of neighbors (like the graph Laplacian). The "FEM" route projects onto the basis of **hat functions** $\psi_i$ (1 at $v_i$, 0 at the other vertices, affine on the faces) and assembles the **stiffness matrix** $L_c$ and the **mass matrix** $M$:
    $$(L_c)_{ij} = \int_{\mathcal M} \langle\nabla\psi_i, \nabla\psi_j\rangle\, dA, \qquad M_{ij} = \int_{\mathcal M} \psi_i\psi_j\, dA .$$
    In practice $M$ is *lumped* to the diagonal of vertex areas $A_i$, and the discrete Laplacian is $\Delta \approx -M^{-1}L_c$. The explicit computation of $(L_c)_{ij}$ on a triangle — an object of ch. 2 — recovers *exactly* the cotangents: FEM and discrete geometry converge.

::: note
[Useful jargon]{.tag} The pair $(L_c, M)$ of ch. 0 is called "stiffness/mass" here (the Gaussian curvature keeps the letter $K$); the convergence of discrete operators toward the smooth Laplace-Beltrami (as the mesh is refined) is subtle — the cotangent one converges in the weak sense (Wardetzky 2007); this is *the* reason why DiffusionNet (ch. 6, ch. 9) prefers to require only *heat operators* from the discrete setting.
:::

## 2. The Laplace-Beltrami operator {#ch2}

On a surface there is no Fourier transform, because there are no translations; the operator that takes its place is the Laplacian of the surface. This chapter builds it on meshes (the cotangent matrix), derives it from an energy, and proves the two properties that make it the central tool of shape analysis: its eigenfunctions act as frequencies, and it does not change when the surface bends without stretching.

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — Laplace-Beltrami]{.tag} The Laplacian *on the surface*:
$$\Delta_{\mathcal M} f = \mathrm{div}_{\mathcal M}(\nabla_{\mathcal M} f).$$
In a local chart with metric $g = (g_{ab})$ (the $g_{ab}$ measure how the chart distorts lengths):
$$\Delta_{\mathcal M} f = \frac{1}{\sqrt{|g|}}\sum_{a,b}\partial_a\!\Big(\sqrt{|g|}\,g^{ab}\,\partial_b f\Big),$$
with $|g| = \det(g_{ab})$ and $(g^{ab})$ the inverse matrix, which recovers $\partial_{xx} + \partial_{yy}$ when $g = I$.

In the discrete setting, the **cotangent stiffness matrix** $L_c$ (symmetric, positive semi-definite):
$$(L_c)_{ij} = \begin{cases} \sum_{l \sim i} w_{il} & i = j\\[2pt] -w_{ij} & j \sim i\\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}, \qquad w_{ij} = \tfrac12\big(\cot\alpha_{ij} + \cot\beta_{ij}\big),$$
where $\alpha_{ij}, \beta_{ij}$ are the angles opposite to edge $(i,j)$. With the lumped mass $M = \mathrm{diag}(A_i)$, the discrete Laplace-Beltrami operator is
$$\Delta \approx -M^{-1}L_c, \qquad (\Delta f)_i \approx \frac{1}{2A_i}\sum_{j \sim i}(\cot\alpha_{ij} + \cot\beta_{ij})\,(f_j - f_i).$$
This area-normalised matrix already contains $M^{-1}$: the eigenproblem uses $L_c$ and $M$ separately (ch. 0), otherwise the mass is divided twice.

Like the graph Laplacian $L = D - A$, the matrix $L_c$ is symmetric positive semi-definite. Its Fourier basis $\{\phi_k\}$ solves
$$L_c\phi_k = \lambda_k M\phi_k, \qquad\text{that is}\qquad \Delta \phi_k = -\lambda_k \phi_k,$$
with increasing $\lambda_k$ (= the "frequencies" of the surface, 1-based: $\lambda_1 = 0$).
:::

::: {#gdl-cotangent .thm}
[Derivation 2.2 — The cotangent operator via the Dirichlet energy]{.tag} The starting point is the Dirichlet energy (the "stiffness" of $f$):
$$E_D(f) = \tfrac12 \int_{\mathcal M} \|\nabla f\|^2\, dA = \tfrac12\sum_{T}\int_T \|\nabla f\|^2\, dA.$$
By approximating $f$ with its barycentric interpolant (affine on each triangle, values $f_i$ at vertices), one gets an exact quadratic form:
$$E_D(f) = \tfrac14 \sum_{i}\sum_{j \sim i} w_{ij}\,(f_i - f_j)^2, \qquad w_{ij} = \tfrac12\big(\cot\alpha_{ij} + \cot\beta_{ij}\big)$$
(each edge is counted twice, once from each endpoint).

The stiffness $L_c$ is the matrix of this quadratic form, $E_D(f) = \tfrac12 f^\top L_c f$:
$$\frac{\partial E_D}{\partial f_i} = \sum_{j\sim i} w_{ij}(f_i - f_j) = (L_cf)_i \approx -A_i\,(\Delta f)_i .$$
In words, $L_c f$ is the gradient of the Dirichlet energy, and $L_c f = 0$ at the interior vertices characterizes the functions of minimal energy (discrete harmonic functions).
:::

::: proof
**Step 1 — gradient of an affine function on a triangle.** On triangle $T = (i,j,k)$, the interpolant is
$$f = f_i\psi_i + f_j\psi_j + f_k\psi_k .$$
Each $\nabla\psi$ is *constant* on $T$, orthogonal to the opposite side, with norm $1/h$ (associated height). In particular
$$\nabla\psi_i + \nabla\psi_j + \nabla\psi_k = 0 .$$

**Step 2 — inner product of two gradients.** Let $h_i, h_j$ denote the heights from $i$ and $j$, and $\theta_k$ the angle at vertex $k$ (opposite to edge $(i,j)$).

The gradient $\nabla\psi_i$ is orthogonal to side $(j,k)$, points toward $i$, and $\|\nabla\psi_i\| = 1/h_i$; likewise $\|\nabla\psi_j\| = 1/h_j$, orthogonal to side $(i,k)$.

The two sides $(j,k)$ and $(i,k)$ making an angle $\theta_k$ with each other, their normals make an angle $\pi - \theta_k$, and the pointing directions flip the sign:
$$\langle\nabla\psi_i, \nabla\psi_j\rangle = -\frac{\cos\theta_k}{h_i h_j} \qquad \text{(constant on } T\text{)}.$$
Then, with $|T|$ the area and $|e|$ the side lengths:
$$\int_T \langle\nabla\psi_i, \nabla\psi_j\rangle\, dA = |T|\cdot\Big(-\frac{\cos\theta_k}{h_i h_j}\Big) = -\frac{|T|\,|e_{jk}|\,|e_{ik}|}{(2|T|)(2|T|)}\cos\theta_k = -\frac{\cos\theta_k}{2\sin\theta_k} = -\frac12\cot\theta_k,$$
where we used $h_i = 2|T|/|e_{jk}|$, $h_j = 2|T|/|e_{ik}|$ and then $|T| = \tfrac12|e_{jk}|\,|e_{ik}|\sin\theta_k$.

**Step 3 — assembly.** Each edge $(i,j)$ belongs to one or two triangles. Sum over these triangles the terms
$$\tfrac12 f_i f_j \int_T\langle\nabla\psi_i,\nabla\psi_j\rangle$$
and reorganize the quadratic form as $\tfrac14\sum_{ij} w_{ij}(f_i - f_j)^2$ (the diagonal terms absorb the off-diagonal ones — exercise 6). The cotangent weights appear, with the contribution $-\tfrac12\cot\theta_k$ of each opposite triangle. [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: key
[Key result — the cotangent weights]{.tag}
$$w_{ij} = \tfrac12\big(\cot\alpha_{ij} + \cot\beta_{ij}\big), \qquad (L_cf)_i = \sum_{j\sim i} w_{ij}(f_i - f_j), \qquad \Delta \approx -M^{-1}L_c$$
:::

::: prop
[Properties (and why they hold)]{.tag}

-   **Symmetry**: $W = (w_{ij})$ is symmetric (each edge carries its weight, constructed symmetrically), so $L_c = L_c^\top$; this is the discrete version of the self-adjointness of ch. 0;
-   **Constants annihilated**: $L_c\mathbf{1} = 0$ because the quadratic form only sees the differences $f_i - f_j$;
-   **Linear precision**: on a *flat* mesh, every affine function (in particular each coordinate $x$, $y$) satisfies $(L_c f)_i = 0$ at the interior vertices — a generic $f$ does not;
-   **Positivity**: $E_D(f) \ge 0$, zero iff $f$ is constant (on each connected component); hence $\lambda_1 = 0$ has multiplicity 1 and $\lambda_2 > 0$ measures the "connectivity" (the Fiedler value of surfaces);
-   **Convergence**: as the mesh is refined, $-M^{-1}L_c$ converges to $\Delta_{\mathcal M}$ in the weak sense — subject to triangle quality (no too-obtuse angles; Wardetzky 2007);
-   **Nodal sets**: the zeros of $\phi_k$ cut the surface into increasingly fine regions as $k$ grows — the "wavefronts" of the surface; $\lambda_k \sim c\,k$ (Weyl's law in dimension 2).
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 2.3 — Heat kernel: spectral construction]{.tag} The solution of the heat equation $\partial_t u = \Delta u$, $u(0) = u_0$, reads (recall $\Delta\phi_k = -\lambda_k\phi_k$ with $\lambda_k \ge 0$)
$$u(t) = e^{t\Delta}u_0 = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}\,\langle \phi_k, u_0\rangle\,\phi_k, \qquad h_t(x, y) = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}\,\phi_k(x)\phi_k(y).$$
Each mode $\phi_k$ is damped by $e^{-\lambda_k t}$: diffusion = spectral low-pass filtering.
:::

::: proof
Direct substitution, term by term (using $\Delta\phi_k = -\lambda_k\phi_k$):
$$\partial_t\big[e^{-\lambda_k t}\langle\phi_k,u_0\rangle\phi_k\big] = -\lambda_k e^{-\lambda_k t}\langle\phi_k,u_0\rangle\phi_k = \Delta\big[e^{-\lambda_k t}\langle\phi_k,u_0\rangle\phi_k\big].$$
At $t = 0$, the sum reduces to $\sum_k\langle\phi_k,u_0\rangle\phi_k = u_0$ (orthonormal basis — for the $M$-weighted inner product of the lab sessions).

The kernel $h_t$ is just the same writing in "integral" form: $u(x,t) = \int h_t(x,y)u_0(y)dy$ (exercise 4). [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 2.4 — Diffusion distances: geometry of the heat kernel]{.tag}
$$D_t^2(x, y) = \|h_t(x, \cdot) - h_t(y, \cdot)\|^2_{L^2} = \sum_k e^{-2\lambda_k t}\,\big(\phi_k(x) - \phi_k(y)\big)^2.$$
Two points are close if their "thermal fingerprints" are close; the exponential weighting short-circuits high frequencies — robust to noise, unlike the geodesic distance. This is the building block of the diffusion geometry of ch. 3.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 2.5 — Isometric invariance (proved)]{.tag} If $T : \mathcal M \to \mathcal N$ is an isometry (preserves the lengths of curves), then for every $f$ on $\mathcal N$ and every $x \in \mathcal M$:
$$\Delta_{\mathcal M} (f \circ T)(x) = (\Delta_{\mathcal N} f)(T(x)).$$
Consequence: identical spectra, transported eigenfunctions — the foundation of all non-rigid shape comparison.
:::

::: proof
An isometry preserves lengths and areas, hence inner products of gradients and integration: for all $u, v$ on $\mathcal N$,
$$\int_{\mathcal N} \langle\nabla u, \nabla v\rangle\, dA_{\mathcal N} = \int_{\mathcal M} \langle\nabla(u\circ T), \nabla(v\circ T)\rangle\, dA_{\mathcal M}$$
(change of variable $T$, Jacobian = 1).

By Green's formula (prop. 0.3 — self-adjointness), for every $v$,
$$\int v\,\Delta_{\mathcal N} u = \int (v\circ T)\,\Delta_{\mathcal M}(u\circ T).$$
Since this holds for every test function $v\circ T$ (surjective), the two Laplacians agree pointwise:
$$\Delta_{\mathcal M}(u\circ T) = (\Delta_{\mathcal N} u)\circ T .$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::

```python
import igl                     # libigl: reference discrete geometry library
import numpy as np
from scipy.sparse.linalg import eigsh

v, f = igl.read_triangle_mesh("bunny.obj")
L_c = -igl.cotmatrix(v, f)      # libigl returns the NSD matrix: negate ONCE -> PSD stiffness
M = igl.massmatrix(v, f, igl.MASSMATRIX_TYPE_VORONOI)   # lumped mass
# generalized problem L_c phi = lambda M phi (shift-invert around 0)
evals, evecs = eigsh(L_c, k=20, M=M, sigma=-1e-8)       # 0 = lambda_1 < lambda_2 <= ...
# visualize evecs[:, k] as a "texture" on the mesh -> vibration modes
# NB: the Dirichlet energy can also be assembled face by face:
G = igl.grad(v, f)              # per-face gradients, shape (3|F|, |V|)
# E_D(f) = 0.5 * sum_T area_T * |grad f|_T^2  (= 0.5 * f @ L_c @ f)
```

::: note
[Why this is the central tool]{.tag}

-   **Isometric invariance**: the spectrum does not change if the surface is "bent" without stretching — *non-rigid* shape comparison (a moving human);
-   **Diffusion**: heat $u(t) = e^{t\Delta}u_0$ — "Can one hear the shape of a drum?": the spectrum encodes the geometry (with honest limits, ch. 3);
-   **Reduced dimension**: projecting onto the first $k$ eigenfunctions ≈ PCA of the surface; all of ch. 4 follows from it.
:::

## 3. Shape descriptors and distances {#ch3}

To compare or match two shapes we need, at each point, a signature that is computable and unchanged when the shape bends. This chapter builds such descriptors from the spectrum of chapter 2 (HKS, WKS, ShapeDNA), together with intrinsic distances, and states the limit of the whole spectral approach.

::: {#gdl-hks .def}
[Definition 3.1 — Heat Kernel Signature (HKS)]{.tag} The amount of residual heat at $x$ after time $t$:
$$\mathrm{HKS}(x, t) = h_t(x, x) = \sum_k e^{-t\lambda_k}\, \phi_k(x)^2$$
— an *intrinsic* descriptor: stable, isometrically invariant; multi-scale (small $t$ = local detail, large = global). These signatures play the role of "features" for correspondence.
:::

::: proof
**Stability (proof sketch).** Perturb the metric by a relative amount $\varepsilon$ (scan noise, different mesh). Two perturbation bounds are used, the second one in the sup norm and for an isolated eigenvalue:
$$|\delta\lambda_k| \le C\varepsilon\lambda_k \ \ \text{(min–max)}, \qquad \|\delta\phi_k\|_\infty \le \frac{C'\varepsilon\lambda_k B_k}{\mathrm{gap}_k}, \qquad B_k = \|\phi_k\|_\infty,$$
where $\mathrm{gap}_k$ is the distance from $\lambda_k$ to the rest of the spectrum.

To first order in $\varepsilon$, each term of the HKS varies as
$$\delta\mathrm{HKS}(x,t) = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}\big(-t\,\delta\lambda_k\,\phi_k(x)^2 + 2\,\phi_k(x)\,\delta\phi_k(x)\big).$$
Bounding each factor pointwise, over the $K$ eigenpairs actually computed:
$$|\delta\mathrm{HKS}(x,t)| \le \varepsilon\sum_{k=1}^{K} e^{-\lambda_k t}\,\lambda_k B_k^2\Big(C\,t + \frac{2C'}{\mathrm{gap}_k}\Big) + O(\varepsilon^2).$$

-   For a fixed $t > 0$ this is a finite sum: the HKS is Lipschitz in the metric — *hence its empirical robustness*. The constant grows as $t \to 0$ (more modes count) and as gaps close.
-   The gaps are an artefact of the eigenfunction route. The HKS only involves the sum of $\phi_k(x)^2$ over each eigenspace, which does not change when the basis of that eigenspace rotates; a perturbation argument on spectral projectors replaces $\mathrm{gap}_k$ by the distance between well-separated *clusters* of eigenvalues.

Note that this computation also justifies the limitation: at large $t$, only the small $\lambda_k$ contribute (a global, not very discriminative descriptor); at small $t$, the series is sensitive to high frequencies (noise); hence the choice of a *logarithmic* grid of $t$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

-   **Scale-normalized HKS**: dilating the shape by $s$ gives $\lambda_k \to s^{-2}\lambda_k$ and $\phi_k \to s^{-1}\phi_k$ (unit norm on an area multiplied by $s^2$), hence
    $$\mathrm{HKS}'(x, t) = s^{-2}\,\mathrm{HKS}(x,\, t/s^2).$$
    Dividing by $\max_x \mathrm{HKS}(x,t)$ removes the amplitude $s^{-2}$ but *not* the rescaled time $t/s^2$. Two fixes:
    -   measure time in units of the shape, $t = \tau\cdot\mathrm{Area}$ or $t = \tau/\lambda_2$, and then normalise the amplitude;
    -   the scale-invariant HKS of Bronstein & Kokkinos (2010): sample $t = \alpha^\tau$, take $\log\mathrm{HKS}$, differentiate in $\tau$ (removes the amplitude), and keep the modulus of its Fourier transform in $\tau$ (removes the shift in $\tau$);
-   **Wave Kernel Signature** (Aubry et al., 2011): a quantum particle of energy $e$ distributed log-uniformly:
    $$\mathrm{WKS}(x, e) = \sum_k \phi_k(x)^2 e^{-(\log e - \log\lambda_k)^2/2\sigma^2}$$
    — a Gaussian window *on a logarithmic scale*: each energy probes one precise frequency band (better localization than the HKS, whose every $t$ mixes low frequencies);
-   **ShapeDNA** (Reuter et al.): the vector $(\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_k)$ — normalized by area — as a global "fingerprint"; $L^2$ distance between fingerprints;
-   **Intrinsic distances**:

    -   *geodesic* (shortest path on the surface): Dijkstra's algorithm on the graph of the mesh (edge lengths) gives an **upper bound** — edge paths are only some of the paths on the surface, and their zigzag error does not vanish when a regular mesh is refined;
    -   continuous refinement (Fast Marching, Kimmel–Sethian) lets paths cross faces and solves the eikonal equation $\|\nabla d\| = 1$ by a growing wavefront, which lowers the Dijkstra estimate toward the true distance;
    -   the modern "heat method" variant (Crane et al.) first solves heat and then takes its renormalized gradient — O(linear solver);
    -   *diffusion distance* (prop. 2.4): truncated spectral approximations of both;

-   **Can one hear the shape of a drum?** No — Gordon, Webb, and Wolpert (1992) constructed pairs of planar domains (polygonal drums) that are *isospectral but not isometric*. The spectrum does not determine the shape: this is a fundamental (and mathematically sound) limit of the whole spectral pipeline — ShapeDNA, spectral constraints of functional maps, HKS.

    In practice: the spectrum discriminates *almost everything*, and one always complements it with operator and descriptor constraints (ch. 4);
-   **Flattening (embedding)**: the first non-constant eigenfunctions give an embedding $x \mapsto (\phi_2(x), \dots, \phi_{k+1}(x))$ that "unfolds" the shape ($\phi_1$ is constant and dropped) — the exact analogue of Laplacian eigenmaps and spectral clustering for graphs ([Graph ML, ch. 4](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch4); spectral positional encodings in Advanced GNN ch. 4 if you take it): same algebra, different object.

## 4. Functional maps {#ch4}

Finding which point of one shape corresponds to which point of another is a huge combinatorial problem. This chapter replaces it with a small linear one: instead of matching points, we transport functions, and in the spectral bases of chapter 2 the map becomes a $k \times k$ matrix.

::: thm
[Theorem/Concept 4.1 — Functional Maps (Ovsjanikov et al., 2012)]{.tag} Instead of looking for the point-to-point correspondence (a combinatorial discrete map, costly), transport *functions* defined on the surfaces:
$$T_F : \mathcal{F}(\mathcal M) \to \mathcal{F}(\mathcal N), \qquad T_F(g) = g \circ T^{-1}$$
Restricted to the spectral bases $\Phi_{\mathcal M}, \Phi_{\mathcal N}$ (the first $k$ eigenfunctions, $M$-orthonormal), the map becomes a **small matrix $C \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times k}$**:
$$b_{\mathcal N} \approx C\, b_{\mathcal M}, \qquad b = \Phi^\top M f, \qquad C_{ij} = \big\langle \phi_i^{\mathcal N},\, T_F\,\phi_j^{\mathcal M}\big\rangle,$$
where $b$ holds the spectral coefficients of a function $f$ and $M$ is the mass matrix of the shape it lives on.
A correspondence of $10^5$ points is replaced by $k^2$ numbers ($k \sim 30$): this is the paradigm shift of the field.
:::

::: key
[Key result — a map between shapes is a small matrix]{.tag}
$$b_{\mathcal N} \approx C\, b_{\mathcal M}, \qquad C \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times k}, \quad b = \Phi^\top M f$$
:::

::: prop
[Constraints 4.2 — what C must satisfy]{.tag}

-   **Descriptor preservation**: if $D_{\mathcal M} \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times q}$ are the coefficients of $q$ descriptors (HKS, WKS...) on $\mathcal M$ and $D_{\mathcal N}$ on $\mathcal N$ (in the same order):
    $$C\,D_{\mathcal M} \approx D_{\mathcal N} \qquad (k \times q \text{ equations});$$
-   **Commutation with operators**:
    $$C\,\Lambda_{\mathcal M} \approx \Lambda_{\mathcal N}\,C$$
    (spectral regularization — the subject of the proof below);
-   **Orthogonality**: if one believes in an isometry, $C^\top C \approx I$. An isometry preserves areas, so $T_F$ preserves the $L^2$ inner products of functions,
    $$\langle T_F f, T_F g\rangle_{\mathcal N} = \langle f, g\rangle_{\mathcal M};$$
    in orthonormal bases the matrix of such a map is orthogonal (exactly for complete bases, approximately after truncation to $k$ functions);
-   **Correspondence coupling**: if a few pairs of points are known, encode them in a 0/1 matrix $\Pi$ with one row per vertex of the second shape and one column per vertex of the first, and $\Pi_{yx} = 1$ when $T(x) = y$. Then $T_F$ acts as $\Pi$ on vertex values, and
    $$C \approx \Phi_{\mathcal N}^\top M_{\mathcal N}\, \Pi\, \Phi_{\mathcal M}$$
    (*hard* constraint vs least squares).
:::

::: proof
**Commutation: proved.** Assume $T : \mathcal M \to \mathcal N$ is an isometry. Theorem 2.5 says that, for every $f$ on $\mathcal N$,
$$\Delta_{\mathcal M}(f \circ T) = (\Delta_{\mathcal N} f)\circ T .$$
Since $T_F^{-1}f = f \circ T$, this is an identity between operators — $T_F^{-1}$ intertwines the two Laplacians — that is
$$T_F\, \Delta_{\mathcal M} = \Delta_{\mathcal N}\, T_F .$$

Apply it to an eigenfunction $f = \phi_j^{\mathcal M}$ of $\mathcal M$, with eigenvalue $\lambda_j^{\mathcal M}$:
$$\Delta_{\mathcal N}\,T_F\phi_j^{\mathcal M} = T_F\,\Delta_{\mathcal M}\phi_j^{\mathcal M} = -\lambda_j^{\mathcal M}\,T_F\phi_j^{\mathcal M} .$$
*The transport of an eigenfunction is an eigenfunction for the same eigenvalue*.

In coefficients, apply the self-adjointness of $\Delta_{\mathcal N}$ (prop. 0.3) to the entry $C_{ij}$ defined in 4.1:
$$-\lambda_i^{\mathcal N}C_{ij} = \langle \Delta_{\mathcal N}\phi_i^{\mathcal N}, T_F\phi_j^{\mathcal M}\rangle = \langle \phi_i^{\mathcal N}, \Delta_{\mathcal N}T_F\phi_j^{\mathcal M}\rangle = -\lambda_j^{\mathcal M}C_{ij}.$$
So
$$C_{ij}\,\big(\lambda_j^{\mathcal M} - \lambda_i^{\mathcal N}\big) = 0,$$
which is entry $(i,j)$ of $C\Lambda_{\mathcal M} = \Lambda_{\mathcal N} C$: $C_{ij} \ne 0$ only if $\lambda_i^{\mathcal N} = \lambda_j^{\mathcal M}$.

If the spectrum is simple, $T_F\phi_j^{\mathcal M} = \pm\phi_j^{\mathcal N}$ and $C$ is diagonal with entries $\pm 1$. Real surfaces are only approximately isometric and multiple eigenvalues create blocks, hence a weak constraint, in the least-squares sense. [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: thm
[Resolution 4.3 — least squares and normal equations]{.tag}
$$C^* = \arg\min_C\ \big\|C D_{\mathcal M} - D_{\mathcal N}\big\|_F^2 + \alpha\big\|C\Lambda_{\mathcal M} - \Lambda_{\mathcal N} C\big\|_F^2 + \beta\big\|C^\top C - I\big\|_F^2 + \mu\|C\|_F^2.$$
Without the orthogonality term, the problem separates over the rows of $C$. The commutativity penalty is a sum over entries,
$$\big\|C\Lambda_{\mathcal M} - \Lambda_{\mathcal N} C\big\|_F^2 = \sum_{i,j} C_{ij}^2\,\big(\lambda_j^{\mathcal M} - \lambda_i^{\mathcal N}\big)^2,$$
so row $i$ (written as a column $c_i$) gets its own diagonal penalty and its own normal equations:
$$c_i = \big(D_{\mathcal M} D_{\mathcal M}^\top + \alpha\,\Omega_i + \mu I\big)^{-1} D_{\mathcal M}\, (d_i^{\mathcal N})^\top, \qquad \Omega_i = \mathrm{diag}\big((\lambda_j^{\mathcal M} - \lambda_i^{\mathcal N})^2\big)_{j=1}^{k},$$
with $d_i^{\mathcal N}$ the $i$-th row of $D_{\mathcal N}$ — $k$ linear systems of size $k \times k$, solved in a few milliseconds.

With orthogonality, one projects onto orthogonal matrices (SVD $C = U\Sigma V^\top$, then $C \leftarrow UV^\top$ — Procrustes projection).
:::

::: prop
[Conversion to point-to-point correspondence + refinement]{.tag} **Soft correspondence**:
$$P = \Phi_{\mathcal N}\, C\, \Phi_{\mathcal M}^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{|V_{\mathcal N}| \times |V_{\mathcal M}|}, \qquad \Pi(x) = \arg\max_y P_{yx}$$
— the matrix $P$ (barely dense, a product of three long matrices) encodes the "probability" that $y$ corresponds to $x$.

**Refinement (the ZoomOut spirit, ch. 9)**: iteratively,

1.  increase $k$ by one notch;
2.  recompute $C$ using the current hard correspondence as a coupling constraint;
3.  re-derive $P$.

The growing spectral resolution acts as *annealing*: large structures settle at small $k$ (strong regularization), details adjust afterwards — algorithm:

```python
C = least_squares(k=k0, descriptors)          # coarse start
for k in range(k0, kmax, step):
    Pi = argmax_per_column(Phi_N[k] @ C @ Phi_M[k].T)   # hard
    C = solve(constraints + coupling(Pi), dim=k)        # soft
return Pi                                          # final correspondence
```
:::

-   **Partial maps**: when only a *part* of $\mathcal M$ corresponds to $\mathcal N$, $T_F$ becomes a restriction; the matrix $C$ is then *rectangular* (or one embeds $\mathcal M$ into $\mathcal N$ via a prolongation operator); the constraints adapt (descriptors only on the visible part);
-   **Learned extensions**: the descriptors $D$ can be produced by a network (FMNet of Litany et al. 2017, then *GeomFMaps* of Donati et al. 2020 — deep geometric functional maps): the network learns descriptors that are *optimal for the matrix C*, the resolution remaining a differentiable least squares; the complete computation graph (network → C → correspondence loss) is trained end to end (Architecture 6.3);
-   **Supervised vs unsupervised**: with annotated pairs (FAUST), one directly supervises $C$ or the geodesic error of $\Pi$; otherwise, one penalizes the structure that $C$ should have — bijectivity, orthogonality, Laplacian commutativity (Architecture 6.3): unsupervised works well for quasi-isometries (humans);
-   **Applications**: *texture transfer*: the texture (a color function!) on $\mathcal M$ is transported by $b_{\mathcal N} = C\,b_{\mathcal M}$ — a matrix multiplication; pose transfer (the correspondence coordinates), morphing;
-   **LLGA connection**: a functional map ≈ an *optimal transport* between reduced bases; shape alignment ≈ graph alignment by Gromov-Wasserstein (box *OT in one page* of ch. 0; [Optimal Transport, ch. 5](../m1p2-optimal-transport/index.html#ch5)); the three languages — GNN, OT, functional maps — describe the same operation of *structural correspondence*.

## 5. Parameterization and processing {#ch5}

Many tasks — texturing, remeshing, editing, reconstruction from a scan — need a surface to be flattened, smoothed or rebuilt. This chapter shows that most of these operations reduce to minimizing an energy built on the Laplacian of chapter 2, hence to solving a sparse linear system.

::: thm
[Harmonic maps — equations proved]{.tag} Flatten a surface with boundary onto the disk $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$: look for $u : \mathcal M \to \mathbb{R}^2$ minimizing the Dirichlet energy $E_D(u) = \tfrac12\int\|\nabla u\|^2$ with the boundary fixed on $\partial\Omega$ (unit circle, uniformly — *Tutte*).
:::

::: proof
First variation: for every perturbation $\delta u$ that vanishes on the boundary,
$$0 = \frac{d}{d\varepsilon}E_D(u + \varepsilon\,\delta u)\Big|_{\varepsilon=0} = \int_{\mathcal M} \langle\nabla u, \nabla\delta u\rangle\, dA = -\int_{\mathcal M} \delta u\,\Delta u\, dA + \oint_{\partial \mathcal M}\delta u\,\partial_n u\, ds.$$
The boundary term vanishes ($\delta u = 0$ on $\partial \mathcal M$). Since $\delta u$ is arbitrary *in the interior*, the minimizer is **harmonic** (component by component):
$$\Delta u \equiv 0 .$$

*Injectivity, smooth case*: the Radó–Kneser–Choquet theorem says that a harmonic map onto a *convex* domain, whose boundary map is a homeomorphism onto the convex boundary, is a diffeomorphism (no folding).

In the discrete setting: the discrete Dirichlet energy (derivation 2.2!) leads to the linear system $(L_c u)_i = 0$ at the interior vertices, with the boundary rows replaced by the constraints — a Poisson solver, a few tens of milliseconds. [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: note
[Discrete injectivity needs positive weights]{.tag} Tutte's theorem (1963), extended by Floater (2003), guarantees a fold-free map when the boundary goes to a convex polygon *and* each interior vertex is a convex combination of its neighbours, i.e. all weights are positive: uniform (Tutte) or mean-value (Floater) weights.

Cotangent weights do not qualify: $w_{ij} < 0$ as soon as $\alpha_{ij} + \beta_{ij} > \pi$, which happens on meshes with obtuse triangles, and the discrete cotangent-harmonic map can then fold. Use mean-value weights when injectivity must be guaranteed, or an (intrinsic) Delaunay mesh, on which the cotangent weights of interior edges are non-negative, and positive in the generic case.
:::

-   **Conformal**: a map is conformal if it preserves *angles* — the local Jacobian is a similarity $du = s\,R$ (Cauchy–Riemann intuition: real and imaginary parts are *conjugate* harmonic); it preserves the shape of small details (textures without shear), but distorts areas;
-   **LSCM — least-squares conformal maps** (Lévy et al. 2002): for a map $(u, v)$, conformality is the Cauchy–Riemann equation $\nabla v = R_{90}\nabla u$ on each face. LSCM minimizes its squared residual, which splits into the Dirichlet energy minus the signed area of the image:
    $$E_{\mathrm{LSCM}}(u,v) = \tfrac12\sum_T |T|\,\big\|\nabla_T v - R_{90}\nabla_T u\big\|^2 = E_D(u) + E_D(v) - \mathcal A(u, v).$$
    The energy is quadratic in $(u,v)$; its minimizer is only defined up to a similarity, so one pins two vertices and solves one sparse linear system. Unlike Tutte, the boundary is free;
-   **ARAP — as-rigid-as-possible**: minimize
    $$E_{\mathrm{ARAP}}(u) = \sum_{T}\min_{R_T \in SO(2)} \big\|J_T(u) - R_T\big\|_F^2,$$
    where $J_T(u)$ is the Jacobian of the map on face $T$ and $R_T$ the "closest" rotation. *Local/global* solver:

    a.  local: each face fixes $R_T = UV^\top$ (SVD of $J_T$);
    b.  global: with the rotations fixed, $E$ becomes quadratic in $u$ → linear system;

    alternate until convergence — a geometric EM; an angle/area compromise without excessive distortion;
-   **Spectral smoothing/filtering**: attenuate high frequencies (denoise), sharpening — signal processing (M1) transported to surfaces;
-   **Deformation: laplacian editing**: move handles while preserving $\Delta\mathbf{x}$ of the positions (the details): minimize $\sum_i\|(L_c\mathbf{x}')_i - (L_c\mathbf{x})_i\|^2$ under constraints — the same machinery as the harmonic map; skinning, morphing — graphics/AR applications of the sister ViCAI module;
-   **Poisson reconstruction**: from a normal field $\mathbf{v}$ (oriented, scan): look for the indicator function $\chi$ of the solid whose gradient best matches $\mathbf{v}$. An exact solution would satisfy
    $$\nabla\chi = \mathbf{v} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \Delta\chi = \mathrm{div}\,\mathbf{v},$$
    but a measured $\mathbf{v}$ is generally not a gradient, so the converse fails. The Poisson equation is the normal equation of $\min_\chi \int\|\nabla\chi - \mathbf{v}\|^2$: it computes the least-squares projection of $\mathbf{v}$ onto gradients. This is the bridge scan → closed mesh;
-   **Decimation — quadric error metric**: associate to each vertex the quadric (sum of the products of the unit plane equations)
    $$Q_i = \sum_{p \in \text{incident planes}} A_p^\top A_p .$$
    The cost of contracting edge $(i,j)$ to the point $\bar v$ is $Q_{ij}(\bar v) = Q_i(\bar v) + Q_j(\bar v)$ — a quadratic form, minimized in closed form; one contracts the lowest-cost edges with a binary heap;
-   **Curvature-based remeshing**: vertex density $\propto$ local curvature (deficit of ch. 1) — allocate the triangle budget where the geometry demands it.

```python
# Spectral smoothing: low-pass filtering on the eigenfunctions
import numpy as np
from scipy.sparse.linalg import eigsh
# L_c, M: stiffness and mass of ch. 2; f: per-vertex function, shape (n,)
evals, evecs = eigsh(L_c, k=200, M=M, sigma=-1e-8)   # 200 modes (ch. 2 kept only 20)
k = 30                                     # keep the 30 lowest frequencies
coef = evecs.T @ (M @ f)                   # spectral coefficients, shape (200,)
coef[k:] = 0                               # axis 0 is the eigen-index: cut modes k+1..200
f_smooth = evecs @ coef
# soft variant: coef *= 1/(1 + (evals/lambda0)**2)  (Butterworth)
# for an (n, d) signal, use coef[k:, :] = 0 and evals[:, None]
```

## 6. Deep learning on surfaces {#ch6}

The networks of image processing assume a regular grid, which point clouds and meshes do not have. This chapter presents the architectures that learn directly on 3D data — PointNet and its local extensions, then DiffusionNet — and the obstacle they all face: a surface has no canonical orientation for a filter.

::: thm
[Architecture 6.1 — PointNet (Qi et al., 2017)]{.tag} Point clouds (without a mesh): per point: shared MLP; global **max** aggregation (permutation-invariant — the same requirement as GNNs, Graph ML module ch. 2); cloud classification/segmentation:
$$f(X) = \rho\Big(\max_{x_i \in X}\ \gamma(x_i)\Big), \qquad |X| = n,\ x_i \in \mathbb{R}^3.$$
:::

::: proof
**Invariance.** A permutation $\pi$ reorders the rows (points) of $X$. The shared MLP $\gamma$ is applied row by row, to each point separately, so it only reorders the rows of $\gamma(X)$; the entrywise max over rows does not depend on their order:
$$f(\pi X) = f(X).$$

*Why max rather than another invariant aggregator?*

-   The product $\prod_i \gamma(x_i)$ is likewise permutation-invariant, but numerically disastrous (explodes toward 0 or $\infty$, unstable multiplicative gradients);
-   the mean is stable but *dilutes* local signals — a discriminative sub-region representing 1% of the cloud is drowned;
-   the max is *selective*: it captures "at least one point exhibits the characteristic", which is exactly the building block of the universal approximation that follows.

**Universality (sketch).** On a compact set $K$, a continuous permutation-invariant function can be uniformly approximated by sums of "soft indicator functions" of balls:
$$g(x) \approx \sum_j c_j\,\mathbb{1}_{B(c_j, r_j)}(x).$$
Now, with $h_\varepsilon$ a steep sigmoid,
$$\mathbb{1}_{B(c,r)}(x) \approx h_\varepsilon(\|x - c\|),$$
and
$$\max_{x_i}\big[1 - h_\varepsilon(\|x_i - c\|)\big]$$
equals \~1 as soon as *a single* point falls in the ball. The union of balls is expressed via the max: PointNet approximates the functions of "membership of at least one point in a ball", the universal building block for compact sets (thm. 1 of the paper). [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: note
[PointNet++ and DGCNN — injecting the local]{.tag} PointNet only sees *unions* of regions (the global max ignores co-localization). Two answers:

-   **PointNet++**:

    a.  *farthest point sampling*: iteratively choose the point farthest from the already chosen centers (uniform coverage, greedy algorithm in $O(n\,k)$);
    b.  *ball query*: group the neighbors in a ball of fixed radius;
    c.  a *local* PointNet per group, then a hierarchy (progressive subsampling — exactly a spatial pooling);

    multi-scale through nested radii;

-   **DGCNN**: *dynamic* k-NN graph in feature space (EdgeConv):
    $$x_i' = \square_{j : (i,j) \in \mathrm{kNN}}\ h_\theta(x_i, x_j), \qquad h_\theta(x_i, x_j) = \mathrm{MLP}\big(x_i,\ x_j - x_i\big),$$
    the max (or mean) over the edges; the graph is rebuilt at every layer — the neighbors drift apart in latent space: a growing receptive field (from local to global, like stacked convolutions).
:::

::: prop
[Geodesic convolutions and the gauge problem]{.tag} A convolution filters a *patch* (geodesic neighborhood, anisotropic). But on a surface, **there is no canonical frame** in the tangent plane: where should "north" go? Every choice of gauge (local rotation of the frame) rotates the filter: an anisotropic filter is not *well-defined*. Three strategies:

-   measure the alignment with an extrinsic direction (the gradient, the normal) — fragile;
-   principal coordinates (eigenframes of the curvature tensor): stable but sign-ambiguous;
-   isotropic filtering (angularly invariant): one gives up anisotropy — this is the spectral answer (filters that are functions of $\Delta$, cf. ChebNet of the Graph ML module) and... the DiffusionNet answer below.
:::

::: thm
[Architecture 6.2 — DiffusionNet (Sharp, Attaiki, Crane, Ovsjanikov — TOG 2022): the block equations]{.tag} Replace convolution with **learned diffusion**. Each block maps per-vertex features $U \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$ (column $u_c$ = channel $c$) to new features of the same width:

1.  **Learned diffusion, one time per channel**: each channel $c$ has its own learned time $t_c > 0$, and
    $$h_c = e^{t_c\Delta}u_c = \Phi\,\mathrm{diag}\big(e^{-\lambda_k t_c}\big)\,\Phi^\top M\,u_c$$
    in a truncated spectral basis (about 128 modes). Small $t_c$ keeps the channel local, large $t_c$ makes it global; no grid of scales is fixed by hand.
2.  **Spatial gradient features (gauge-invariant)**: at each vertex $i$, the tangent gradient of every diffused channel, written in an arbitrary local frame as a complex number, gives $z_i \in \mathbb{C}^d$. With a learned complex matrix $A \in \mathbb{C}^{d \times d}$,
    $$g_i = \tanh\Big(\mathrm{Re}\big(\overline{z_i} \odot A z_i\big)\Big) \in \mathbb{R}^d .$$
    Rotating the frame by an angle $\theta$ multiplies every entry of $z_i$ by $e^{-\mathrm{i}\theta}$. The factor cancels between $\overline{z_i}$ and $Az_i$, so $g_i$ does not depend on the frame; the raw gradient does, which is why it is never used directly.
3.  **Per-vertex MLP with a residual**: $u \leftarrow u + \mathrm{MLP}\big([u,\ h,\ g]\big)$ at each vertex — a *pointwise* operator (no gauge!).
4.  Stack a few blocks (4 blocks of width 128 by default), between an input and an output linear layer.

**Properties**: discretization-agnostic (only a Laplacian, a mass matrix and a tangent gradient are required — available on meshes *and* on point clouds, through the point-cloud Laplacian of Sharp & Crane 2020); isotropic diffusion (no gauge) + inner products of gradients for directional information; learned scales; state of the art on FAUST/SCAPE at the time, robust to re-meshings — the "discrete element" of the field.
:::

::: note
[DiffusionNet in practice: the training recipe]{.tag}

-   **Precompute once per shape, and cache**: center the shape and scale it to unit area; compute the mass $M$, about 128 eigenpairs of $L_c\phi = \lambda M\phi$, and the tangent-gradient operators. This is the only costly step (seconds per mesh); training then only multiplies small dense matrices.
-   **Inputs**: either raw XYZ, with a random rotation of each training shape at each step (augmentation, since XYZ is not rotation-invariant), or 16 HKS values on a log-spaced time grid, which are intrinsic and need no rotation augmentation.
-   **Loss by task**: classification — mass-weighted mean over vertices, then cross-entropy; segmentation — per-vertex cross-entropy; correspondence — a functional-map head (Architecture 6.3), supervised by the ground-truth map or with the unsupervised loss.
-   **Optimizer and test**: Adam with learning rate $10^{-3}$ and step decay. Always also evaluate on *remeshed* test shapes, never seen in training: that is the robustness claim to check.
:::

::: thm
[Architecture 6.3 — Learned functional maps (level 3)]{.tag} Put the network *before* the functional map of ch. 4 and train through it.

1.  A feature extractor $F_\theta$ (DiffusionNet) produces $q$ descriptors per vertex on both shapes, $G_{\mathcal M} = F_\theta(\mathcal M)$ and $G_{\mathcal N} = F_\theta(\mathcal N)$, with shared weights.
2.  Project them on the spectral bases, as in Theorem 4.1:
    $$D_{\mathcal M} = \Phi_{\mathcal M}^\top M_{\mathcal M}\,G_{\mathcal M}, \qquad D_{\mathcal N} = \Phi_{\mathcal N}^\top M_{\mathcal N}\,G_{\mathcal N} \qquad (k \times q).$$
3.  **Functional-map layer**: solve Resolution 4.3 row by row in closed form (with the per-row penalty $\Omega_i$). A linear solve is differentiable, so gradients reach $\theta$:
    $$c_i = \big(D_{\mathcal M}D_{\mathcal M}^\top + \alpha\,\Omega_i\big)^{-1}D_{\mathcal M}\,(d_i^{\mathcal N})^\top .$$
4.  **Supervised loss** (GeomFMaps, Donati, Sharma & Ovsjanikov 2020): $\|C - C_{\mathrm{gt}}\|_F^2$, with $C_{\mathrm{gt}}$ built from the ground-truth point map as in Constraints 4.2.
5.  **Unsupervised loss** (Roufosse, Sharma & Ovsjanikov 2019): compute $C_{\mathcal M\mathcal N}$ and $C_{\mathcal N\mathcal M}$ and penalize what a near-isometry implies:
    $$\mathcal L = w_{b}\big\|C_{\mathcal N\mathcal M}C_{\mathcal M\mathcal N} - I\big\|_F^2 + w_{o}\big\|C_{\mathcal M\mathcal N}^\top C_{\mathcal M\mathcal N} - I\big\|_F^2 + w_{l}\big\|C_{\mathcal M\mathcal N}\Lambda_{\mathcal M} - \Lambda_{\mathcal N}C_{\mathcal M\mathcal N}\big\|_F^2,$$
    plus the same terms with the roles of the shapes swapped: bijectivity, orthogonality, Laplacian commutativity.
6.  At test time, convert $C$ into a point map and refine it with ZoomOut (ch. 4, ch. 9).

*Why it works*: the network no longer has to output a correspondence for $10^4$ vertices; it only has to make the $k \times k$ problem of ch. 4 well posed. The structure of $C$ (ch. 4) becomes the training signal.
:::

-   **Transformers on surfaces**: global attention between points/vertices with *intrinsic* positional encodings (HKS, random geodesic distances) as the positional add-on: the GPS recipe transplanted. A GPS layer (Rampášek et al. 2022) adds, with residuals and normalization, a local message-passing update and a global self-attention update over all nodes, then applies an MLP; positional encodings (Laplacian eigenvectors, random-walk statistics, or here the HKS) are concatenated to the input features. Details in Advanced GNN ch. 5 if you take it; quadratic cost → hierarchical subsampling;
-   **Self-supervised learning**: geometric pretexts — predict descriptors (HKS: "know thyself"), local orientation, reconstruct masked regions; contrastive pre-training between views/poses of the same shape (as PointContrast, Xie et al. 2020, does for point clouds): LLM pre-training applied to surfaces;
-   **Benchmarks**:
      Dataset          Task                                   Metric
      ---------------- -------------------------------------- ----------------------------
      FAUST / SCAPE    human correspondence (various poses)   mean geodesic error (×100)
      SHREC            shape retrieval                        mAP
      ModelNet40       cloud classification                   accuracy
      ShapeNet-parts   part segmentation                      mIoU

```python
# Mesh classification via LBO-features + small classifier (lab skeleton)
import torch
# features: (n, 7) = [Gauss_curvature, Mean_curvature, HKS(t1..t5)] per vertex
encoder = torch.nn.Sequential(
    torch.nn.Linear(7, 128), torch.nn.ReLU(),
    torch.nn.Linear(128, 64),
)
head = torch.nn.Linear(64, n_classes)                     # classification head
pooled = encoder(features).max(dim=0).values              # (64,): max over VERTICES (dim 0)
logits = head(pooled).unsqueeze(0)                        # (1, n_classes)

# DiffusionNet "learned diffusion" (Architecture 6.2): one time per channel
class LearnedDiffusion(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d):
        super().__init__()
        self.t = torch.nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(d))       # softplus(t) > 0, one per channel
    def forward(self, H, evals, evecs, mass):             # H: (n, d); evecs: (n, k); mass: (n,)
        H_spec = evecs.T @ (mass[:, None] * H)            # (k, d) spectral coefficients
        t = torch.nn.functional.softplus(self.t)          # (d,)
        decay = torch.exp(-evals[:, None] * t[None, :])   # (k, d): e^{-lambda_k t_c}
        return evecs @ (decay * H_spec)                   # (n, d); parentheses matter
```

## 7. Euclidean equivariance {#ch7}

A rotated or translated molecule is the same molecule, and a network should not have to learn this from data. This chapter defines equivariance, recalls the EGNN layer proved equivariant in Graph ML, and asks what invariance means for point clouds and surfaces — where bending adds a symmetry that rotations alone do not cover.

::: def
[Definition 7.1 — Equivariance and invariance]{.tag} A group $G$ acts on inputs and outputs through representations $\rho_{\mathrm{in}}(g)$ and $\rho_{\mathrm{out}}(g)$. A map $f$ is *equivariant* if
$$f\big(\rho_{\mathrm{in}}(g)\,x\big) = \rho_{\mathrm{out}}(g)\,f(x) \qquad \forall g \in G,$$
and *invariant* if $\rho_{\mathrm{out}}$ is trivial: $f(\rho_{\mathrm{in}}(g)x) = f(x)$. For clouds/meshes, the natural group is $E(n)$: an element $(Q, t)$ with $Q \in O(n)$ (rotations and reflections) acts on each point as $x \mapsto Qx + t$. A rotated molecule remains the same molecule — the network should neither relearn every orientation, nor confuse them.
:::

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Recall — EGNN (Satorras, Hoogeboom, Welling, ICML 2021), proved in Graph ML
:::

State: positions $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^n$, features $h_i$. Layer:
$$m_{ij} = \phi_e\big(\|x_i - x_j\|^2,\ h_i, h_j\big), \qquad x_i' = x_i + \sum_{j \ne i} (x_i - x_j)\,\phi_x(m_{ij}), \qquad h_i' = \phi_h\big(h_i, \textstyle\sum_j m_{ij}\big).$$

-   **Why it works**: $Q$ is orthogonal, so distances, hence messages and $h_i'$, are invariant; the position update is a sum of differences $x_i - x_j$, each mapped to $Q(x_i - x_j)$, so $x' \mapsto Qx' + t$.
-   **Full proof**: [Graph ML, ch. 8, Proposition 8.3](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch8); Ex. 5 below asks you to redo it in the notation of this page.
::::

-   **Point clouds**: PointNet on raw XYZ (ch. 6) is permutation-invariant but *not* rotation-invariant. Three cures, in increasing strength: random-rotation augmentation (approximate, learned from data), invariant inputs (distances, angles), or layers that are equivariant by construction (EGNN, SE(3)-transformers);
-   **Surfaces**: intrinsic objects — $\Delta_{\mathcal M}$, its spectrum, the HKS, DiffusionNet fed with HKS — are invariant to rigid motions *and* to isometric bending, a much larger symmetry than $E(3)$. DiffusionNet fed with XYZ is not, hence the rotation augmentation of the recipe in ch. 6. Its gradient features (Architecture 6.2) are invariant to a *local* change of tangent frame — a gauge symmetry, the surface cousin of $E(n)$ equivariance;
-   **Equivariance vs invariance**: for classification, invariance suffices (max pooling) — but to *generate* or *localize*, one needs equivariance (to output positions consistent with the inputs); the same debate as "final aggregation vs messages" in GNN theory;
-   **SE(3)-transformers (sketch)**: for the continuous version, attention is built on *equivariant fields* (irreducible representations; invariant keys/queries, vector-valued values) — the machinery exceeds this course, but the principle stands: invariant similarities, transformed values;
-   **E(2)-symmetric routing**: in a routing problem on a 2D map (travelling salesman, vehicle routing), the optimal tour does not change when the customer coordinates are rotated, reflected or translated. Sym-NCO (Kim, Park & Park, NeurIPS 2022) trains a neural solver with a REINFORCE baseline shared across rotated copies of each instance, plus a regularizer that makes the encoder's embedding rotation-invariant — augmentation turned into a training signal. The Year 2 dispatcher subject of the [transverse project](../m2-projet-transverse/index.html) (Y2.4) builds on it;
-   **Connection with the Advanced GNN module, ch. 8**: EGNN is a GNN whose messages are constrained by geometry — "geometry first, network second"; the generation of conformers by EGNN (positions = equivariant output) meets diffusion models (the three-line DDPM recall is in ch. 8).

## 8. Applications and LLGA connections {#ch8}

This chapter gathers where the tools of the module are used — molecules, proteins, industry, shape generation — and then works out, for self-study, three bridges to the graph and LLM tracks of the master.

-   **3D molecules**: a molecule is an equivariant cloud (EGNN, ch. 7) — conformer prediction (equilibrium geometries minimize energy); generation by equivariant diffusion, where an EGNN is the denoiser (EDM, Hoogeboom et al. 2022; see the recall below, [Graph Generative Models, ch. 5](../m2-graph-generative-models/index.html#ch5) for EDM among the diffusion models and [ch. 8](../m2-graph-generative-models/index.html#ch8) for the applications); properties (solubility, toxicity) via geometric descriptors (molecular HKS/WKS);
-   **Proteins**: binding interfaces = correspondence of *molecular surfaces* (shape complementarity — partial functional maps); docking; geometry meets the master's molecule-graph pipeline (Graph ML);
-   **Industry**: CAD/mesh retrieval, 3D scanning (reverse engineering: Poisson reconstruction of ch. 5), quality control by comparison to tolerances, dental/orthopedics (crowns = quasi-isometric shapes); autonomous vehicles (lidars = clouds → PointNet++/DGCNN); AR/VR: avatars (human body correspondence — FAUST in production), mesh compression (spectral coordinates);
-   **Shape generation**: diffusion on point clouds and meshes (noising/denoising positions and connectivities — the DDPM recalled below, in $\mathbb{R}^{3n}$ with equivariance); the "shape-GPT" future: surface tokens.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
DDPM in three lines (full treatment: Deep Learning P1 9.4 or Deep Learning P2 7.3)
:::

Noise the data $x_0$ in closed form, with a schedule $\beta_t$, $\alpha_t = 1 - \beta_t$ and $\bar\alpha_t = \prod_{s \le t}\alpha_s$:
$$x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}\,\varepsilon, \qquad \varepsilon \sim \mathcal N(0, I).$$
Train a network to predict the noise, then sample by running the learned denoising steps from $x_T \sim \mathcal N(0, I)$ back to $x_0$:
$$\mathcal L(\theta) = \mathbb E_{t,\,x_0,\,\varepsilon}\,\big\|\varepsilon - \varepsilon_\theta(x_t, t)\big\|^2 .$$
For 3D point sets, take $\varepsilon_\theta$ to be an EGNN acting on centered positions: the generated distribution is then invariant to rotations. Links: [Deep Learning (P1), ch. 9](../m1p1-deep-learning/index.html#ch9), [Deep Learning (P2), 7.3](../m1p2-deep-learning-p2/index.html#dl-generative), [Multimodal GenAI, ch. 3](../m1p2-multimodal-genai/index.html#ch3).
::::

### Worked bridges (self-study, ≈ 2 h) {#bridges}

Three worked examples connect the module to graphs and to language. Each one reuses a chapter almost verbatim, and each one is the seed of a Year 2 transverse-project subject.

**Bridge A — the HKS on a graph Laplacian.** A graph has no metric, but it has a Laplacian $L = D - A$ (symmetric positive semi-definite, 1-based spectrum, [Graph ML, ch. 4](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch4)). It plays the role of $L_c$, with $M = I$, and Definition 3.1 carries over unchanged: $\mathrm{HKS}(v,t)$ is the heat that stays at node $v$ after time $t$.

Two things change. Graphs have no physical scale, so measure time in units of $1/\lambda_2$ and normalise each time column — the scale normalisation of ch. 3. And graphs can be large: there, compute only the low end of the spectrum with a sparse shift-invert solver, and check what it returns. Lanczos can return fewer copies of a repeated eigenvalue than its multiplicity, and leaves hanging on the same node, frequent in real graphs, create exactly such repeats. On the 77-node example below, the dense solver is exact and instant.

```python
import numpy as np, networkx as nx
from scipy.sparse.linalg import eigsh

G = nx.les_miserables_graph()                     # 77 characters, weighted co-appearance graph
L = nx.laplacian_matrix(G).astype(float)          # L = D - A: sparse, PSD (plays L_c, M = I)
lam, phi = np.linalg.eigh(L.toarray())            # all 77 eigenpairs, ascending
# large graph: lam, phi = eigsh(L, k=200, sigma=-1e-3), then check repeated eigenvalues
ts = np.geomspace(0.1, 10, 8) / lam[1]            # time grid in units of 1/lambda_2
hks = (phi**2) @ np.exp(-np.outer(lam, ts))       # (n, 8): HKS(v, t)
hks /= hks.sum(axis=0, keepdims=True)             # amplitude normalisation per time
nodes = list(G.nodes())
print([nodes[i] for i in np.argsort(-hks[:, 0])[:3]])   # most heat kept at small t
```

At small $t$ the heat stays longest at peripheral characters of degree 1 — low degree means slow leakage. Jondrette and MlleVaubois come first; then six characters seen only with Myriel tie exactly (they are twins, see Bridge B), so which of them is printed third depends on rounding.

These leaves make $\lambda = 1$ an eigenvalue of multiplicity 9. A 30-mode `eigsh` run often misses some of its copies, and the ranking then changes from run to run: the warning above, observed. Used as node features, these columns are a structural encoding of the kind studied in [Advanced GNN, ch. 4](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html#ch4).

On a knowledge graph (Y2.1) or a transaction graph (Y2.5), the stability bound of ch. 3 suggests that a few injected edges move the HKS little. Treat this as a hypothesis to test, not a theorem: the bound is for small perturbations, and one edge can be a large perturbation of a sparse graph.

**Bridge B — graph alignment by functional maps.** Two graphs on the same entities, with an unknown node correspondence (two snapshots of a network, two knowledge graphs over shared entities), are two "shapes". Ch. 4 applies verbatim: eigenbases of both Laplacians, HKS columns as the functions to preserve, $C$ by Resolution 4.3, then a one-to-one node map. This is the pipeline of GRASP (Hermanns et al., 2021), without its base-alignment step.

The protocol needs gold correspondences: take $G_2$ as a randomly permuted copy of $G_1$, optionally with a fraction of its edges removed, and score the fraction of nodes mapped to their true partner.

```python
from scipy.optimize import linear_sum_assignment
def basis(G, k):                                  # dense eigh: fine below ~5,000 nodes
    Ld = nx.laplacian_matrix(G, nodelist=range(len(G))).toarray().astype(float)
    lam, phi = np.linalg.eigh(Ld); return lam[:k], phi[:, :k]
def hks_cols(lam, phi, q=16):
    return (phi**2) @ np.exp(-np.outer(lam, np.geomspace(0.1, 10, q) / lam[1]))
def fmap(D1, D2, l1, l2, alpha=1e-3, mu=1e-6):    # Resolution 4.3, one Omega_i per row
    k = len(l1)
    return np.stack([np.linalg.solve(D1 @ D1.T + alpha * np.diag((l1 - l2[i])**2)
                                     + mu * np.eye(k), D1 @ D2[i]) for i in range(k)])

G1 = nx.convert_node_labels_to_integers(nx.karate_club_graph())
perm = np.random.default_rng(0).permutation(len(G1))   # gold: node u of G1 is perm[u] in G2
G2 = nx.relabel_nodes(G1, dict(enumerate(perm)))        # remove a few edges here for noise
l1, P1 = basis(G1, 30); l2, P2 = basis(G2, 30)
C = fmap(P1.T @ hks_cols(l1, P1), P2.T @ hks_cols(l2, P2), l1, l2)
cost = ((P2[:, None, :] - (P1 @ C.T)[None, :, :])**2).sum(-1)  # delta functions, mapped by C
rows, cols = linear_sum_assignment(cost)                # node rows[i] of G2 <-> cols[i] of G1
print("accuracy", np.mean(perm[cols] == rows))
```

-   On Zachary's karate club (34 nodes, weighted edges) this recovers every node without noise. With 5% of the edges removed (4 of 78, graph kept connected), it averages about 85%, with a wide spread: from about 73% to 94% over 60 random draws.
-   On Les Misérables it reaches only about 80% even without noise (75–92% across random permutations). Eleven of the 77 characters are exact twins — six seen only with Myriel, five only with Valjean, all with the same edge weight — and no structural method can tell twins apart. Guessing within each group caps the expected accuracy at about 88%: report this ceiling next to the accuracy.
-   Removing edges can disconnect a graph, which adds zero eigenvalues and breaks the spectral matching: align the largest connected components.

**Bridge C — 3D + language: contrastive text–shape retrieval.** The CLIP objective of [LLM 8.2b](../m2-large-language-models/index.html#vlm) works with a shape tower in place of the image tower.

-   **Towers**: a shape encoder $f_\theta$ — PointNet (Architecture 6.1) on 2,048 points sampled on the surface, or DiffusionNet — followed by a linear projection; a *frozen* pretrained text encoder $g$ followed by a trainable projection; both outputs are $\ell_2$-normalised. A few thousand captioned shapes cannot train a language model, so the shape tower learns to land in the text space.
-   **InfoNCE in three lines**: for a batch of $B$ pairs $(x_i, y_i)$ and a temperature $\tau$ (about 0.07, often learned),
    $$s_{ij} = \frac{\langle f_\theta(x_i),\, g(y_j)\rangle}{\tau}, \qquad \mathcal L = -\frac{1}{2B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\Big[\log\frac{e^{s_{ii}}}{\sum_{j} e^{s_{ij}}} + \log\frac{e^{s_{ii}}}{\sum_{j} e^{s_{ji}}}\Big].$$
    Each row and each column of $S = (s_{ij})$ is a $B$-way classification whose correct class is the diagonal.
-   **Data**: ABO, Amazon Berkeley Objects (Collins et al., CVPR 2022), about 8,000 artist-made 3D models of real products with their catalogue listings; use the product title and category as the caption, and split by product.
-   **Metric**: Recall@$k$ for text → shape, the fraction of text queries whose shape is among the $k$ nearest shape embeddings, for $k = 1, 5, 10$; then again on remeshed or resampled test shapes, the robustness question of ch. 6.
-   **Towards an LLM**: the projected shape embedding can enter an LLM as a soft token through a trained projector, as images do in LLM 8.2b — the "3D tokens" idea made concrete, and the shape tower of the Y2.3 subject.

```python
import torch.nn.functional as F
zs = F.normalize(proj_s(pointnet(points)), dim=-1)       # (B, d) shape embeddings
zt = F.normalize(proj_t(text_encoder(titles)), dim=-1)   # (B, d); text_encoder frozen
S = zs @ zt.T / tau                                      # (B, B) similarities
y = torch.arange(len(S))
loss = 0.5 * (F.cross_entropy(S, y) + F.cross_entropy(S.T, y))   # InfoNCE, both directions
```

## 9. Course research notes — Geometric Data Analysis (Ovsjanikov) {#ch9}

Maks Ovsjanikov heads the *Geometric Data Analysis* group at LIX (École Polytechnique). The four publications below are not merely "references" for this course: they *are* the course — every chapter from 2 to 6 stems directly from them.

::: thm
[Functional Maps — SIGGRAPH 2012 (the founding paper)]{.tag} M. Ovsjanikov, M. Ben-Chen, J. Solomon, A. Butscher, L. Guibas, [arXiv:1204.3967](https://arxiv.org/abs/1204.3967) — Best Paper Award.

**The story.** Before 2012, shape correspondence was handled *point to point*: combinatorial matching of tens of thousands of vertices, fragile heuristics. The idea: represent the map as a *linear operator on functions* (ch. 4), which becomes a small matrix in spectral bases.

**Beyond chapter 4.** The paper also introduces: the effective computation of the constraints, the inverse conversion (matrix → correspondence), and above all the demonstration that *a few well-chosen constraints* suffice (descriptors + commutation).

**Extensions (by the hundreds)**: dense coupling, partial maps, the *shape Differences* formulation (comparing how two shapes transport functions), and the ZoomOut refinement below.

**Positioning.** It is one of the most influential papers of modern shape analysis; the framework is today the standard *and* the basis of learned methods (GeomFMaps).
:::

::: thm
[HKS — Sun, Ovsjanikov, Guibas, SGP 2009]{.tag} [A Concise and Provably Informative Multi-Scale Signature](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1467-8659.2009.01515.x).

**The genesis.** The heat kernel $h_t(x, y)$ (ch. 2) transports information between points; its *diagonal* $h_t(x,x)$ — the heat that returns to its starting point — is a descriptor of $x$ at every scale $t$.

**Contributions.**

1.  the multi-scale characterization (small $t$ = local, large = global);
2.  the proof of isometric invariance *and* stability (the proof sketch of ch. 3);
3.  the analysis of the space of scales.

**Impact.** The HKS and its WKS variant are the input descriptors of almost all correspondence pipelines (including functional maps); the scale-invariant version extends it to heterogeneous scans.
:::

::: thm
