[ZoomOut — SIGGRAPH Asia 2019]{.tag} S. Melzi, J. Ren, E. Rodolà, A. Sharma, P. Wonka, M. Ovsjanikov, [arXiv:1904.07865](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.07865).

**Problem.** The spectrum truncated to $k$ eigenfunctions is a trade-off: small $k$ = robust but coarse; large $k$ = precise but noisy.

**Idea.** The iterative spectral refinement of ch. 4: reconstruct a *hard* correspondence at resolution $k$, reinject it as a coupling constraint at resolution $k + \Delta$, and repeat. The regularization emerges from the upsampling rhythm; no additional data is required.

**Results.** Substantial improvements on mediocre initial correspondences, near-zero cost (matrix products); it became the standard post-processor.

**Positioning.** The "soft ↔ hard" loop is the geometric ancestor of iterative refinements; its spirit resurfaces in the local/global solvers of ch. 5.
:::

::: thm
[DiffusionNet — TOG 2022]{.tag} N. Sharp, S. Attaiki, K. Crane, M. Ovsjanikov, [arXiv:2012.00888](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.00888).

**Problem.** All "CNN-like" architectures on surfaces depend on the discretization (mesh vs cloud, resolution) and run into the gauge problem (ch. 6).

**Idea.** A minimal and geometrically honest layer: diffusion with one *learned* time per channel + gauge-invariant gradient features + pointwise MLP — block equations in ch. 6 (Architecture 6.2).

**Results.** State of the art at publication on FAUST/SCAPE correspondence (also when training on one dataset and testing on the other), SHREC'11 classification and human-body segmentation; demonstrated robustness to discretization changes; works on point clouds without a mesh, through the point-cloud Laplacian of Sharp & Crane (2020).

**Positioning.** The prototype of "sober geometric deep learning": instead of adapting convolution to the surface, inject the physical *operator* (heat) as a learning building block — the convergence of chapters 2 (operators) and 6 (networks).
:::

::: note
[The common thread]{.tag} HKS (2009: eigenfunctions as descriptors) → Functional Maps (2012: the map as an operator) → ZoomOut (2019: spectral refinement) → DiffusionNet (2022: the operator inside the network): fifteen years of research that follow exactly the progression of this course — from the spectral to deep learning.
:::

## Exercises {#ex}

1.  **★ Cotangents.** Verify that the stiffness matrix $L_c$ is symmetric and that $L_c\mathbf{1} = 0$. On a flat mesh, check that the coordinate functions are discretely harmonic — $(L_c x)_i = (L_c y)_i = 0$ at every interior vertex (linear precision) — whereas a generic $f$, such as $\sin(3x)\,y^2$, gives $L_c f \ne 0$.
2.  **★ Gauss–Bonnet on the cube.** Verify numerically theorem 1.3 on the cube meshed into 12 triangles; what happens to the sum of deficits if each face is subdivided into 4? (answer: unchanged — why?).
3.  **★ Spectrum = fingerprint.** Compute the first 20 eigenvalues of $\Delta$ for two rigid shapes and their articulated (bent) versions; plot the superimposed spectra and comment on the isometric invariance.
4.  **★ Heat kernel and PDEs.** Verify that $h_t(x, y) = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_k t}\phi_k(x)\phi_k(y)$ solves $\partial_t h_t = \Delta_y h_t$, $h_0(x, y) = \delta_x(y)$, and deduce that $u(t) = e^{t\Delta}u_0$ diffuses any initial condition.
5.  **★ EGNN invariance.** In the EGNN equations recalled in ch. 7, show that the messages $m_{ij}$ depend only on distances that are invariant under $E(n)$, and that the position update is equivariant; compare your proof with Graph ML, Proposition 8.3.
6.  **★★ Stiffness of a triangle.** On a triangle $T = (i, j, k)$ with hat functions $\psi_i, \psi_j, \psi_k$, show that
    $$\int_T \langle\nabla\psi_i, \nabla\psi_j\rangle\, dA = -\frac12\cot\theta_k,$$
    where $\theta_k$ is the angle at vertex $k$, opposite to edge $(i,j)$.
7.  **★★ HKS.** Show that $\mathrm{HKS}(x, t)$ is isometrically invariant; compute and visualize multi-scale HKS on a FAUST human — identify the "self-descriptive points" (hands, head).
8.  **★★ Toy functional map.** Two known isometric meshes: build $C$ by least squares (descriptor + commutation constraints); reconstruct the correspondence; measure the mean geodesic error; what happens if $k$ is too small?
9.  **★★ Spectral commutation.** Show that if $T : \mathcal M \to \mathcal N$ is an isometry, then $T_F \Delta_{\mathcal M} = \Delta_{\mathcal N} T_F$, and that in the eigenbasis this forces $C\Lambda_{\mathcal M} \approx \Lambda_{\mathcal N} C$ — hence the structure (almost block-diagonal over clusters of close eigenvalues) of $C$.
10. **★★ PointNet invariance.** Show that max pooling *and* the product are permutation-invariant, but that the product is numerically unstable (explosion/underflow of multiplicative gradients) while the mean dilutes local signals; implement the three aggregators and check on a permuted cloud (stability + selectivity of a discriminative sub-region).
11. **★★★ DiffusionNet vs GCN.** On FAUST (correspondence): compare a GCN on the graph of the mesh vs DiffusionNet (learned diffusion times); discuss why diffusion is a good geometric "mixer".
    -   *Data*: FAUST (Bogo et al., CVPR 2014; free registration at faust.is.tue.mpg.de): 100 registered human scans, 10 people × 10 poses, all with the same 6,890-vertex template, so vertex $i$ of one scan corresponds to vertex $i$ of every other — the ground truth. Train on scans 0–79, test on 80–99.
    -   *Robustness set*: the remeshed FAUST of Ren et al. (2018), about 5,000 vertices per shape with different connectivities, distributed with its correspondences to the template.
    -   *Setup*: `pip install torch potpourri3d robust_laplacian`, clone `github.com/nmwsharp/diffusion-net`, precompute and cache the operators once (recipe of ch. 6); a free GPU tier is enough.
    -   *Protocol*: both networks output per-vertex features fed to the functional-map head of Architecture 6.3; report the mean geodesic error, normalised by the square root of the area, on the original and on the remeshed test shapes.
12. **★★★ Project.** Shape retrieval: extract (HKS, spectrum, curvatures) → aggregation → similarity by optimal transport ($W_1$ on descriptor distributions); evaluate the mAP on a subset of SHREC; the three connections of the course at work.
    -   *Data*: the SHREC'11 non-rigid track (Lian et al., 2011), 600 watertight meshes in 30 classes of 20 shapes in various poses. A subset of 10 classes × 20 shapes is enough; the simplified versions distributed with MeshCNN (Hanocka et al., 2019) load in seconds.
    -   *Pipeline*: per shape, normalise to unit area and compute 100 eigenpairs; then the HKS (16 times, ch. 3), the WKS, ShapeDNA (the first 50 eigenvalues) and a histogram of the angle deficit (ch. 1). Compare two shapes by $W_1$ between their area-weighted HKS distributions with POT's `ot.emd2` (box *OT in one page*, ch. 0).
    -   *Evaluation*: each shape queries the 199 others; report the mean average precision (mAP) and compare with the baseline ShapeDNA + Euclidean distance.

::: note
[Solution 1 — Symmetry and constants]{.tag} Each edge weight $w_{ij} = \frac12(\cot\alpha_{ij} + \cot\beta_{ij})$ is constructed symmetrically in $i, j$ (the two opposite angles favor neither endpoint): $W = W^\top$.

And $L_c\mathbf{1} = 0$ because the diagonal term of each row $i$ is the opposite of the sum of the off-diagonal entries:
$$\sum_{j\sim i}w_{ij} - \sum_{j\sim i}w_{ij} = 0 .$$

On a flat mesh, only *affine* functions have a zero discrete Laplacian at the interior vertices (linear precision of the cotangent weights). For a coordinate $x$, $(L_cx)_i = \sum_j w_{ij}(x_i - x_j) = 0$ at every interior vertex, even on an irregular Delaunay mesh (numerically about $10^{-14}$). A generic $f$, such as $\sin(3x)\,y^2$, gives values of order 1. At boundary vertices the one-ring is incomplete and $(L_c\mathbf{x})_i \ne 0$: it points along the in-plane normal to the boundary.
:::

::: note
[Solution 2 — Gauss–Bonnet on the cube]{.tag} Each corner receives three angles of $\pi/2$:
$$\text{deficit } 2\pi - 3\times\frac{\pi}{2} = \frac{\pi}{2}, \qquad \text{total } 8\times\frac{\pi}{2} = 4\pi = 2\pi\chi \text{ with } \chi = 2.$$
The vertices added by subdivision (the edge midpoints, inside a square face or on a crease of the cube) are flat — their angles sum to $2\pi$, zero deficit — and the 8 corners keep their $\frac{\pi}{2}$: the sum is *unchanged*.

This illustrates that the right-hand side of Gauss–Bonnet is topological; it is a practical integrity test for a closed mesh: $\sum_iK_iA_i = 2\pi\chi$ whatever the resolution.
:::

::: note
[Solution 4 — The heat kernel solves the PDE]{.tag} Term-by-term derivative:
$$\partial_t h_t(x,y) = -\sum_k\lambda_ke^{-\lambda_kt}\phi_k(x)\phi_k(y),$$
and $\Delta_yh_t(x,y)$ gives the same sum after applying $\Delta\phi_k = -\lambda_k\phi_k$ to the second factor — equal.

As $t \to 0$, $h_t(x,\cdot) \to \delta_x$ (an approximate identity family, orthonormal basis); by superposition, $u(t) = e^{t\Delta}u_0$ with each mode damped by $e^{-\lambda_kt}$.
:::

::: note
[Solution 6 — Stiffness of a triangle]{.tag} **Case $i \ne j$**: redo step 2 of derivation 2.2. $\nabla\psi_i$ is constant, orthogonal to the opposite side, with norm $1/h_i$; the angle between $\nabla\psi_i$ and $\nabla\psi_j$ equals $\pi - \theta_k$, hence
$$\int_T\langle\nabla\psi_i,\nabla\psi_j\rangle dA = |T|\cdot\big(-\frac{\cos\theta_k}{h_ih_j}\big) = -\frac12\cot\theta_k$$
(via $h_i = 2|T|/|e_{jk}|$, $h_j = 2|T|/|e_{ik}|$, $|T| = \frac12|e_{jk}||e_{ik}|\sin\theta_k$).

**Case $i = j$**:
$$\int_T\|\nabla\psi_i\|^2 dA = |T|/h_i^2 = \frac{|e_{jk}|}{2h_i} = \frac12(\cot\theta_j + \cot\theta_k),$$
because the height from $i$ splits the opposite side into segments $h_i\cot\theta_j$ and $h_i\cot\theta_k$ (an algebraic identity, also valid for obtuse angles via the signs of the cotangents).
:::

::: note
[Solution 7 — HKS invariance]{.tag} By theorem 2.5 (proved invariance), $\phi_k^{\mathcal N} \circ T$ is an eigenfunction of $\mathcal M$ for $\lambda_k^{\mathcal N}$. The spectra coincide after sorting and, if the eigenvalues are simple, $\phi_k^{\mathcal N}(Tx) = \pm\phi_k^{\mathcal M}(x)$. Then
$$\mathrm{HKS}_{\mathcal N}(Tx,t) = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_kt}\phi_k^{\mathcal N}(Tx)^2 = \sum_k e^{-\lambda_kt}\phi_k^{\mathcal M}(x)^2 = \mathrm{HKS}_{\mathcal M}(x,t)$$
(the square kills the sign; for multiple eigenvalues: equality after a basis rotation within each eigenspace).

On FAUST: at small $t$, extremities (hands, head) = self-descriptive points; at large $t$, convergence toward the constant component — hence the logarithmic grid in $t$.
:::

::: note
[Solution 9 — Commutation and the structure of C]{.tag} With $T_F(g) = g \circ T^{-1}$, we have $T_F^{-1}f = f \circ T$, so Theorem 2.5 gives
$$\Delta_{\mathcal M}T_F^{-1} = T_F^{-1}\Delta_{\mathcal N}, \qquad\text{that is}\qquad T_F\Delta_{\mathcal M} = \Delta_{\mathcal N}T_F .$$
The proof of 4.2 then establishes, for simple spectra,
$$T_F\phi_j^{\mathcal M} = \pm\phi_{\sigma(j)}^{\mathcal N} \quad\text{with}\quad \lambda_j^{\mathcal M} = \lambda_{\sigma(j)}^{\mathcal N} .$$
In coefficients, $C_{ij}$ vanishes unless $\lambda_j^{\mathcal M} = \lambda_i^{\mathcal N}$: the matrix of $T_F$ in eigenbases is block-diagonal — $C_{ij} \ne 0$ only if $\lambda_i^{\mathcal N}$ and $\lambda_j^{\mathcal M}$ coincide.

For quasi-isometric surfaces, the equalities become proximities: the soft constraint $\|C\Lambda_{\mathcal M} - \Lambda_{\mathcal N}C\|_F^2$ encodes this structure, locks the frequency correspondences, and blocks spectrally absurd matchings. Limitation: close or multiple eigenvalues leave undecided blocks — resolved by the descriptor constraints.
:::

::: note
[Solution 10 — PointNet aggregators]{.tag} Max and product are permutation-invariant (reordering a set changes neither its max nor its product); experiment confirms this on a permuted cloud. But:

a.  the product of $n$ factors below 1 collapses (underflow) and multiplies the gradients — unstable;
b.  the mean is stable but dilutes: if 1% of the cloud carries the discriminative signal, it drowns it where the max captures it;
c.  the max learns local "detectors" — the building block of universality (proof of 6.1).
:::

## Projects and assessment {#projects}

The official assessment is not displayed: the SynapseS 2026–2027 sheet of this course unit is not yet published, and the master's wiki gives only its volume (24 h), credits (2 ECTS) and instructor. Everything below is therefore a proposal: project subjects at the scale of a course project, a written exam and a rubric.

The projects exercise mainly O4 (graph-structured and geometric data) and O6 (3D data as a modality), O5 (graphs × language) through the worked bridges of ch. 8, and O7 (hands-on work on real datasets) throughout. They are course-sized versions of the Year 2 transverse-project subjects (Y2.1–Y2.5), which all draw on this module.

### Solo projects {#projects-solo}

1.  **[Solo · ≈ 25 h] Why matching collapses under remeshing.** Papers: Sharp, Attaiki, Crane and Ovsjanikov (2022), DiffusionNet; Melzi et al. (2019), ZoomOut.
    -   *Question*: which correspondence pipelines survive a change of mesh, and why do the others fail — the collapse described in the introduction?
    -   *Work*: on FAUST and its remeshed version (setup of Ex. 11), compare a GCN on raw XYZ, HKS/WKS functional maps (Resolution 4.3), the same refined by ZoomOut, and DiffusionNet with a functional-map head (Architecture 6.3). Plot the mean geodesic error against $k$ and against mesh resolution, and explain each failure with ch. 2 (graph Laplacian vs cotangent Laplacian, eigenvalue drift across meshes).
    -   *Success*: a table original vs remeshed for the four pipelines over 3 seeds, in which every degradation larger than the seed spread is explained by a measured cause.
    -   *Deliverables*: code, 4–6 page report, 10-minute talk. Chapters: [ch. 2](#ch2), [ch. 3](#ch3), [ch. 4](#ch4), [ch. 6](#ch6).

2.  **[Solo · ≈ 25 h] Equivariant 3D molecular property prediction.** Paper: Satorras, Hoogeboom and Welling (2021), EGNN. Connects this course to [Graph ML, ch. 8](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch8) and [Graph Generative Models, ch. 8](../m2-graph-generative-models/index.html#ch8).
    -   *Question*: how much training data does built-in $E(3)$ equivariance save on molecular property prediction?
    -   *Work*: implement an EGNN layer (recall of ch. 7) and test its equivariance with random orthogonal matrices and translations. On QM9 (Ramakrishnan et al., 2014; `torch_geometric.datasets.QM9`), predict the HOMO–LUMO gap with the EGNN and with a non-equivariant GNN fed raw coordinates, with and without rotation augmentation, for 1k, 5k and 20k training molecules.
    -   *Success*: learning curves over 3 seeds; an equivariance error at float precision (relative error below $10^{-5}$ in float32); a clear statement of where augmentation closes the gap and where it does not. Stretch goal: an EGNN denoiser for a tiny conformer DDPM (recall of ch. 8).
    -   *Deliverables*: code, 4–6 page report, 10-minute talk. Chapters: [ch. 7](#ch7), [ch. 8](#ch8).

3.  **[Solo · ≈ 20 h] From raw scans to texture transfer.** Papers: Kazhdan, Bolitho and Hoppe (2006), Poisson reconstruction; Lévy et al. (2002), LSCM.
    -   *Question*: how much distortion does each flattening method introduce, and can a functional map carry a texture from one person to another?
    -   *Work*: from two raw FAUST scans (FAUST ships raw scans next to the registrations), run Poisson reconstruction and quadric decimation (Open3D); cut a disk-like patch and flatten it with Tutte (uniform weights), cotangent-harmonic, LSCM and ARAP maps; measure angle and area distortion and count folded triangles. Then transfer a texture between the two registrations with a functional map (ch. 4).
    -   *Success*: a four-method distortion table; a fold count per method — zero for uniform weights, as Tutte guarantees, and for cotangent weights the folds, if any, traced to negative-weight edges (perturb the patch to create obtuse triangles if none occur); a texture-error map against the ground-truth correspondence.
    -   *Deliverables*: code, 4–6 page report, 10-minute talk. Chapters: [ch. 4](#ch4), [ch. 5](#ch5).

1.  **[Group of 3 · ≈ 30 h each] Spectral shape retrieval with optimal transport.** Papers: Mémoli (2011), Gromov–Wasserstein distances and the metric approach to object matching; Reuter, Wolter and Peinecke (2006), ShapeDNA. Connects this course to [Optimal Transport, ch. 5](../m1p2-optimal-transport/index.html#ch5).

Ablate the time grid, $k$ and the entropic regularisation; probe isospectral pairs (the Gordon–Webb–Wolpert drums, meshed in 2D) and near-isometric failure cases.

Connects this course to [Graph ML, ch. 4](../m1p2-graph-ml/index.html#ch4) and [Advanced GNN, ch. 4](../m2-advanced-gnn/index.html#ch4); seed of the Y2.1 subject.
    -   *Question*: how far does Bridge B go on real networks with noise, and what do GRASP's extra steps buy?
    -   *Work*: SNAP graphs (ego-Facebook, 4,039 nodes; CA-GrQc, 5,242 nodes), each permuted with 0–5% of its edges removed, largest connected component kept. Implement Bridge B with sparse eigensolvers, then GRASP's base alignment and a ZoomOut-style refinement; compare with a Hungarian matching on HKS columns alone.
    -   *Split*: data and noise protocol; spectral pipeline and refinement; evaluation, twin ceiling and scaling to $10^4$ nodes.
    -   *Success*: accuracy-vs-noise curves over 5 seeds with the twin ceiling marked, and a measured answer to "which step brings which gain".

### Written exam (proposal) {#projects-exam}

Two hours, one handwritten A4 sheet allowed, no electronic device; four questions.

1.  **Question (5 points).** A matching pipeline built on raw XYZ coordinates works on test shapes in the training pose, but fails on bent poses and on remeshed copies. Explain both failures, name the tools of the course that fix each one, and give one limit of these fixes. *Expected*: XYZ is extrinsic, so it changes under rotation and isometric bending, while the spectrum and the HKS are intrinsic (Theorem 2.5). A graph Laplacian depends on connectivity; the cotangent Laplacian converges to $\Delta_{\mathcal M}$ and DiffusionNet needs only operators. Limits: isospectral shapes, intrinsic symmetries, scale, multiple eigenvalues.

2.  **Question (7 points).** A regular octahedron with unit edges has its six vertices at $(\pm r, 0, 0)$, $(0, \pm r, 0)$, $(0, 0, \pm r)$, with $r = 1/\sqrt2$.

    (a) Compute the angle deficit at each vertex and check Theorem 1.3. (b) Compute the cotangent weight $w_{ij}$ of an edge and the barycentric area $A_i$. (c) Compute $H_i\mathbf{n}_i = \tfrac12(M^{-1}L_c\mathbf{x})_i$ at $(r, 0, 0)$ and compare with the circumscribed sphere.

    *Expected*: (a) four angles of $\pi/3$ meet at each vertex, so the deficit is $2\pi/3$, and
    $$6 \times \frac{2\pi}{3} = 4\pi = 2\pi\chi, \qquad \chi = 6 - 12 + 8 = 2 .$$

    (b) Both opposite angles are $60°$, so $w_{ij} = \tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{2}{\sqrt3} = 1/\sqrt3$. Four triangles of area $\sqrt3/4$ meet at each vertex, so $A_i = 4 \cdot \tfrac13 \cdot \tfrac{\sqrt3}{4} = 1/\sqrt3$.

    (c) The four neighbours of $(r,0,0)$ are $(0,\pm r,0)$ and $(0,0,\pm r)$; their differences with the vertex sum to $(4r, 0, 0)$, so
    $$(L_c\mathbf{x})_i = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}\,(4r, 0, 0), \qquad H_i\mathbf{n}_i = \tfrac12\sqrt3\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt3}(4r,0,0) = (\sqrt2, 0, 0).$$
    The normal points outward and $H_i = \sqrt2 = 1/r$, exactly the mean curvature of the circumscribed sphere.

3.  **Question (5 points).** Let $T : \mathcal M \to \mathcal N$ be an isometry and $T_F(g) = g \circ T^{-1}$, and let $C$ be its matrix in orthonormal eigenbases, as in Theorem 4.1:
    $$C_{ij} = \big\langle\phi_i^{\mathcal N},\, T_F\phi_j^{\mathcal M}\big\rangle .$$
    (a) Prove that $C\Lambda_{\mathcal M} = \Lambda_{\mathcal N}C$. (b) Prove that $C^\top C = I$ when complete bases are used.

    *Expected*: (a) Theorem 2.5 gives $T_F\Delta_{\mathcal M} = \Delta_{\mathcal N}T_F$. Compute one inner product in two ways, using the self-adjointness of $\Delta_{\mathcal N}$:
    $$-\lambda_i^{\mathcal N}C_{ij} = \big\langle \Delta_{\mathcal N}\phi_i^{\mathcal N}, T_F\phi_j^{\mathcal M}\big\rangle = \big\langle \phi_i^{\mathcal N}, T_F\Delta_{\mathcal M}\phi_j^{\mathcal M}\big\rangle = -\lambda_j^{\mathcal M}C_{ij}.$$
    Hence, for all $i, j$,
    $$C_{ij}\big(\lambda_j^{\mathcal M} - \lambda_i^{\mathcal N}\big) = 0,$$
    which is the entrywise form of $C\Lambda_{\mathcal M} = \Lambda_{\mathcal N}C$.

    (b) An isometry preserves areas, hence the inner products of functions. By Parseval in the complete basis of $\mathcal N$:
    $$(C^\top C)_{jl} = \sum_i C_{ij}C_{il} = \big\langle T_F\phi_j^{\mathcal M}, T_F\phi_l^{\mathcal M}\big\rangle = \big\langle \phi_j^{\mathcal M}, \phi_l^{\mathcal M}\big\rangle = \delta_{jl}.$$

4.  **Question (3 points).** In DiffusionNet, the gradient of a feature at a vertex is a complex number $z$ written in an arbitrary tangent frame. Show that $z$ depends on the frame but $g = \mathrm{Re}(\bar z\,a z)$, with a learned $a \in \mathbb{C}$, does not. Why does the diffusion step need no frame at all?

    *Expected*: rotating the frame by $\theta$ maps $z$ to $e^{-\mathrm{i}\theta}z$, so $z$ itself rotates, while
    $$\overline{e^{-\mathrm{i}\theta}z}\;a\,e^{-\mathrm{i}\theta}z = e^{\mathrm{i}\theta}e^{-\mathrm{i}\theta}\,\bar z\,a z = \bar z\,a z .$$
    Diffusion $e^{t\Delta}$ acts on scalar functions through the intrinsic, isotropic operator $\Delta$: no direction is ever chosen.

### Grading rubric (proposal) {#projects-rubric}

| Criterion | Weight | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Understanding of the method and the theory | 25 % | Correct statement of the method, its invariances and its assumptions, linked to the chapters used |
| Implementation and reproducibility | 25 % | Correct, readable code; fixed seeds and scripts that regenerate every figure; operators cached as in the recipe of ch. 6 |
| Experiments | 25 % | The success criterion reached or the gap explained; an honest baseline; robustness to remeshing or noise measured, not assumed |
| Analysis and critical view | 15 % | Failure cases traced to a cause (symmetry, isospectrality, connectivity, scale); one proposed improvement |
| Report and talk | 10 % | Clear structure, readable figures, talk within time, precise answers to questions; in groups, each member presents their part |
